t: The Bureaucracy and the Policy Agenda
abs: The public administration literature has been dominated by questions about how politicians can control the bureaucracy’s application and implementation of laws at the back end of the policy process. Much less scholarly attention is devoted to the influence of the bureaucracy on the content and composition of the policy agenda at the front end of the process. Agenda setting is a fundamental aspect of politics, and this article examines the influence of the bureaucracy on the policy agenda and the conditions for this influence. The core proposition is that the policy agenda is larger and more diverse in political systems in which administrative professionals take up a larger share of the bureaucracy. This effect is expected to be mitigated by the involvement of elected representatives in the policymaking process. The empirical analysis supports these expectations. The findings are based on a time-series cross-section dataset from 98 Danish municipalities over 7 years containing a detailed coding of local council agendas and rich register data.

t: Contracting, Civil Service Reform, and the Call to Reprofessionalize Public Service
abs: Paul Verkuil’s book Valuing Bureaucracy: The Case for Professional Government narrates the changing composition of the federal workforce and calls for the “reprofessionalization” of public service in the United States. He builds on the arguments presented in his 2007 book Outsourcing Sovereignty: Why Privatization of Government Functions Threatens Democracy and What We Can Do About It to make the case that the proliferation of contracting is, in part, to blame for the devaluation of public service. He contends outsourcing contributes to “deprofessionalizing” civil servants and argues for striking the right balance between career public managers and contractors. He describes the flaws in the US civil service system and the need for reform. Verkuil is clearly concerned about the future of government and public service. Verkuil draws from personal experience in the US federal service. He served as President Obama’s appointee as Chairman of the Administrative Conference of the United States (ACUS), an independent agency with public and private representatives charged with improving regulatory and administrative processes. He is also an administrative law scholar, president emeritus of the College of William and Mary, and former dean of both the Tule University Law School and the Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law. As in Outsourcing Sovereignty, his approach to Valuing Bureaucracy is through a legal lens, yet he couples this with his practical experience at ACUS to define problems and design solutions. The book begins by conceptually connecting contracting to civil service reform. At the outset, Verkuil asserts the rise of contracting is not simply an ideological preference for smaller government, but rather it is also a practical attempt to overcome obstacles in hiring and firing. He also uses salient examples, such as the use of private prisons, to highlight the accountability problems that result from relying on contractors instead of professional civil servants. The second part of Verkuil’s book addresses the need to reform the civil service. Verkuil provides a brief history of the federal civil service in the United States and then identifies problems with the current system. He focuses primarily on the Senior Executive Service and managerial personnel not in collective bargaining units, which centers the discussion on strategic issues related to recruiting, hiring, retaining, and terminating. Verkuil’s experiences with bureaucratic processes while at ACUS inform his description of how strategic managers perform workarounds to avoid onerous processes when staffing agencies. Although the book primarily focuses on dynamics in federal agencies, Verkuil pauses to profile state government failures that contribute to public distrust in government, such as the water crisis in Flint, Michigan, to underscore the need for professionalization throughout all levels of government. The book ends with proposed solutions to improve and reprofessionalize government. Verkuil’s tidy prescriptions are primarily adopted from the Partnership for Public Service and the National Academy of Public Administration (NAPA), where he is also a fellow. He leverages the NAPA 2016 transition report, which provided 10 administrative proposals for the incoming presidential administration. The report included solutions to modernize the civil service through collaboration, strategic goal-setting, data-driven decision making, transparency, and employee-engagement in performance management. Verkuil builds on the NAPA proposals by specifying priorities to foster innovation, leverage technology, improve coordination, among others. Valuing Bureaucracy is less about providing a full account of issues related to contracting or civil service reform and more about illustrating the breadth of obstacles to effective public service. He addresses tenure, veteran’s preferences, unions, A-76 programs, and in-sourcing inherently governmental functions, among many other topics that influence or are affected by the deprofessionalization of public service. As a result, the book provides an accessible case for civil service reform that is well suited for an introductory course on bureaucracy. Verkuil’s arguments are clear and concise. Valuing Bureaucracy can provide students with an understanding of the relationship between contractors and bureaucrats, the need for professional civil servants, and inform key personnel issues. Although administrative law is Verkuil’s expertise, he acknowledges that research in the fields of public administration and public policy are better positioned to speak to the practice of government, which is the focus of the book. Verkuil relies heavily on accounts from the popular press to substantiate his arguments and seldom utilizes empirical work in public administration to buttress his arguments (e.g., the book has only about a half dozen references from the Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory, Public Administration Review, and Review of Public Personnel Administration). In this regard, the book is more relevant for classroom use than research. For example, Verkuil’s prescriptions for reform speak to motivating and incentivizing civil servants. He could have explored how goal ambiguity and goal misalignment might contribute to motivation and performance challenges (Chun and Rainey 2005). Verkuil also missed an opportunity to explore the research on public service motivation and “new public service” or values-based management, which speak directly to motivation and incentives (Bryson et al. 2014; Perry et al. 2010). Verkuil cites the loss of graduates entering government from Princeton and Harvard, noting more now enter the private sector than the public sector. I also see increasing numbers of students from public affairs programs choosing employment in the private and nonprofit sectors, and there is a growing dialogue on the matter in the Journal of Public Affairs Education. Two important dynamics are in play that are not explored in the book. Public administrators are increasingly contract managers, overseeing service delivery performed by nonprofit and private sector personnel. Thus, students interested in direct service delivery are likely to work on contract, not as public employees. And students of public affairs seldom graduate with the technical training necessary to effectively manage contracts, which exacerbates the problems Verkuil identifies. Overall, Verkuil persuades the reader that the federal workforce infrastructure is in serious need of repair, drawing parallels to the United States’ dilapidated bridges, roads, and physical infrastructure. The metaphor is powerful, illustrating how continued disregard of professionalized public service will further erode public trust in government.

t: Citizen-Based Brand Equity: A Model and Experimental Evaluation
abs: Government agencies carry reputations in the public imagination. Agency names, images, and icons help form a brand that conveys information about that agency’s competency in a given area of public policy. This article brings the concept of consumer-based brand equity from business marketing to public administration research on agency reputation. Like their commercial counterparts, public organizations may enjoy positive brand equity that provides political leverage and facilitates effective management, or negative brand equity that weakens an agency politically and frustrates administration. Just as different commercial products appeal to different kinds of consumers, an agency’s brand value might differ with various segments of the public. We adapt a classic model of consumer branding to the public administration context, developing a framework for analyzing citizen-based brand equity for public agencies. A series of experiments embedded in a national survey is then used to gauge brand favorability for four US federal agencies as first-order test of the concept. We find consistent evidence that agencies’ brands positively affect support for federal management, but also that partisanship conditions agencies’ brand favorability.

t: Opening up the Black Box of Organizational Rule Effectiveness
abs: The importance of organizational rules can hardly be overstated. Rules provide a blueprint for organizational design, define the goods and services that organizations are required to deliver, and ensure that employees understand what is expected of them, to mention just a few examples. Indeed, organizations would be rife with uncertainty, inefficiencies, and favoritism in the absence of rules. Although much research in public administration is concerned with rules that do not work (e.g., red tape), Leisha DeHart-Davis argues that understanding rules that do work is equally important for scholars and practitioners alike. This is a valid point, especially if we consider that academic bodies of research can (or, perhaps, should) meaningfully inform practice. In this light, a comprehensive overview of how organizational rules can be created, implemented, and enforced effectively is most welcome. Creating Effective Rules in Public Sector Organizations not only provides a thorough review of the academic state of the art on organizational rule effectiveness but is also highly readable, making it suitable for multiple audiences. In Creating Effective Rules in Public Sector Organizations, DeHart-Davis puts forward an organizational rules framework that incorporates three perspectives: organizational, individual, and behavioral. The organizational perspective considers rules as an enabler of organizational functions such as coordination, empowerment, and socialization. The individual perspective looks at how individuals experience rules. For example, rules can signal procedural fairness to organizational members, level status differences within the organization, or convey trust between management and employees. Finally, the behavioral perspective captures a wide variety of rule behaviors, ranging from overcompliance to prosocial rule breaking. DeHart-Davis does a good job of synthesizing the different strands of literature from public administration, organization studies, and social psychology underlying the three perspectives. Overall, the perspectives put forward are convincing and appropriate. Theoretical discussions are nicely illustrated with descriptive data from the Local Government Workplaces Study (LGWS), which is a research endeavor that has enabled DeHart-Davis to collect qualitative and quantitative data from local government organizations over a 10-year period. Although the text is well written and informative, it would have been insightful to also see a more extensive discussion of why these particular dimensions are included in the framework and not others, especially given the “panoramic perspective” (p. 17) of the framework. Notably, relatively little attention is paid in the book to the role of external stakeholders and external rules as factors influencing the creation and implementation of organizational rules. DeHart-Davis uses the case of organizational grievance policies to highlight the value added of using three perspectives to study the same policy issue before moving on to a discussion of so-called green tape theory. In a nutshell, green tape reflects the characteristics of effective organizational rules. For example, written rules are considered to be more effective than unwritten rules because written rules convey legitimacy and validity, whereas unwritten rules are often seen as invalid and arbitrary. The concept of green tape, which has already been theoretically refined and tested in a number of journal articles, is particularly appropriate for a book on effective rules. Surprisingly, the three perspectives outlined in the first part of the book are not explicitly included as such in the chapter on green tape. Rather, the assumption is that green tape characteristics contribute to rule effectiveness in general, and will therefore have similar impacts across the three perspectives. This assumption may hold in many cases, but not always. Consulting stakeholders in the process of rule creation may improve perceptions of procedural fairness but at the same time create procedural delays that are detrimental to organizational performance. Similarly, it seems unlikely that managers are able to efficiently communicate rule purposes to every individual employee. Creating effective rules is itself a costly process in which the benefits do not necessarily outweigh the costs. Green tape theory seems to signify a best-case scenario in which resources are not constrained and stakeholder goals are perfectly aligned. In practice, this situation is likely to be the exception rather than the rule. As a result, more could possibly have been said about rulemaking under conditions of budget constraints, divergent stakeholder goals, etc. One of the book’s most interesting sections is the discussion of the Five-Second Rule, an informal crowd control policy used by the Missouri police in the context of the Ferguson riots in 2014. The Five-Second Rule required that peaceful protesters stand still for more no more than 5 s to avoid being arrested. The rule was later challenged in federal court, and DeHart-Davis uses a green tape perspective to convincingly show that this particular rule was lacking in all five green tape characteristics. That is, the rule was not in writing, illogically designed, inconsistently applied, over-controlling, and had poorly understood purposes. The Five-Second Rule provides a helpful real-life application of green tape theory but also highlights the inherent difficulty associated with identifying effective rules. Rather than provide an example of a very effective rule that incorporates green tape characteristics, DeHart-Davis uses the Five-Second Rule to show how the absence of green tape characteristics is associated with an ineffective rule. The problem here is that—much like the performance of a referee in a major sporting event—we only tend to notice rules when something goes wrong. Few memorable anecdotes start with the phrase, “you would not believe what an incredibly effective rule I encountered today.” This issue may seem trivial at first glance, but it has important implications for empirical research on rule effectiveness as the most effective organizational rules likely remain largely unnoticed by definition. In the final chapter of the book, DeHart-Davis reflects on how the organizational rules framework may inform future research. Unfortunately, this section is rather short and generic. For example, DeHart-Davis mirrors calls from the red tape literature to focus more strongly on citizens when studying rule effectiveness. This point is valid, but less so in the context of the organizational rules framework which seems primarily concerned with internal stakeholders. DeHart-Davis’s suggestion of studying organizational rule stocks in terms of red tape and green tape ratios is innovative, but there is little discussion as to what such a research endeavor would look like. This feels like an omission, as a strong argument can be made that green tape, red tape, and administrative burden are actually variations on the same underlying theme, namely rule effectiveness. A more extensive discussion of how these different research streams fit within the organizational rules framework (or not) and how they may be studied empirically could have been another valuable contribution of the book. In sum, Creating Effective Rules in Public Sector Organizations succeeds in synthesizing the diverse and disparate literatures on rule effectiveness. The three perspectives of the organizational rules framework capture a large part of the theoretical spectrum and are intuitively appealing. The book is well written and very accessible for both scholars and practitioners. The absence of a fully-fledged research agenda is a missed opportunity, but there is more than enough theoretical material in the book for future studies to test and further refine the organizational rules framework.

t: The Governance of Goal-Directed Networks and Network Tasks: An Empirical Analysis of European Regulatory Networks
abs:
In this article, we answer the research question “What factors affect the structural complexity of 
network administrative organizations (NAOs)?” The question warrants further research because 
of the lack of empirical studies on the topic. We design a quantitative study of the structure of all 
37 European regulatory networks. Using Bayesian statistics, we analyze the new data set and test 
hypotheses, derived from the literature, about the factors affecting the structural complexity of 
NAOs. We find that networks with rule-setting tasks are strongly related to less complex NAOs, 
whereas networks with member-sanctioning and rule-enforcing tasks are strongly related to more 
complex NAOs. Theoretically, network-level tasks appear to affect NAO complexity, particularly 
given the implied uncertainty of those tasks, as well as the network-level operational requirements 
related to them.

t: The Determinants of Promotion to High Public Office in Germany: Partisan Loyalty, Political Craft, or Managerial Competencies?
abs: The politicization of bureaucracy is a widespread strategy to increase the political control of ministerial departments in parliamentary democracies. It is, however, largely unknown why executive politicians promote some officials rather than others to high public office. Based on a unique dataset of all senior officials in German federal ministries and agencies that held office in the period 1997–2015, this article investigates whether partisan loyalty, political craft, and managerial competencies influence the chance of promotion to the highest civil service position in Germany (state secretary). We apply event history modeling to draw inferences on the relative importance of different selection criteria used by ministers when recruiting state secretaries from a candidate pool of senior officials. A key finding is that ministers consistently prefer politically loyal to nonloyal candidates. Although ministers also consider candidates’ political craft and selected managerial competencies, they are likely to trade-off partisan loyalty against those qualifications. The article contributes to the literature on politicization in the public sector by comparing potential and actual office holders and by including a broad set of selection criteria, moving beyond the literature’s dominating focus on partisan loyalty. The methodological approach developed in this article may well be transferred to other institutional contexts and used for comparative studies in this area.

t: Challenges and Opportunities: The 21st Century Public Manager in a VUCA World
abs: In The 21st Century Public Manager, Zeger Van Der Wal addresses various challenges that public managers face, reflecting upon a world characterized by volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity (VUCA). Government organizations and officials are increasingly met with distrust and cynicism from their constituents, while the demand for more resilient, effective, and accountable public action continues to rise. Despite this tense climate, there are few practical guides for future public managers. In that sense, this book is a welcome addition to theory and practice. As the challenges and potential threats are grave, Van der Wal carefully and persuasively posits that public managers must understand the nature of challenges while removing the barriers that led to them, noting that these very challenges can turn into immense opportunities depending on “how public managers can prepare for and respond to a VUCA world” (p. 5). Van der Wal emphasizes the role of public managers solving public problems through cooperation across multiple stakeholders and organizations from multiple sectors, and supports his arguments by providing ample cases and tracing a history of failures and successes.

t: More Than Public Service: A Field Experiment on Job Advertisements and Diversity in the Police
abs: There is a human capital crisis looming in the public sector as fewer and fewer people show interest in government jobs. At the same time, many public sector organizations struggle with increasing the diversity of their workforce. Although many institutional forces contribute to the challenge, part of the solution is in how government recruits. This study presents the results of a field experiment aimed at attracting more and different people to apply to a police force by varying job advertisements in a postcard. The results suggest that focusing on public service motivation (PSM) messages is ineffective at attracting candidates that would not have applied anyway. Rather, messages that focus on the personal benefits of applying to the job—either emphasizing the challenge of the job or the career benefits—are three times as effective at getting individuals to apply as the control, without an observable loss in applicant quality. These messages are particularly effective for people of color and women, thereby supporting a key policy goal of the police to increase diversity of applicants.

t: Cross-Sector Collaboration for Public Innovation
abs: Jacob Torfing wrote Collaborative Innovation in the Public Sector for both scholars and practitioners in the field of public administration and policy. In the book, he ambitiously aims to develop an integrative framework to explore how network-based collaboration between state and nonstate stakeholders generates innovation “by combining theoretical and empirical insights in systematically analyzing the key aspects of the processes of collaboration innovation” (p. 13). Public innovation refers to “an intended but inherently contingent process that involves the development and realization, and frequently also the spread, of new and creative ideas that challenge conventional wisdom and disrupt the established practices within a specific context” (p. 30). To help further understand innovation conceptually, Torfing suggests seven types of innovation related to public administration and policy: product innovation (newly developed products to meet citizens’ unmet needs), service innovation (new forms of public service or new ways of service delivery), process innovation (novel processes for producing public service), organizational innovation (new forms and ways of organizing public organizations), governance innovation (new modes of governing collaboration between public organizations and external stakeholders), policy innovation (novel policy tools and assessment tools), and discourse innovation (new languages and symbols to identify social problems or to change the image of public organizations). Most importantly, Torfing suggests a theory of collaborative innovation. To develop this analytical model of collaborative innovation, he reviews and combines a wide range of theoretical and empirical insights from innovation theory, theories of network governance, institutional theory, systems and complexity theory, theories of learning, and discourse theory. The analytical model consists of five key dimensions: initial conditions, institutional arenas of interaction, public innovation outputs, evaluation of outcomes, and metagovernance. First, he takes into consideration three levels (macro, meso, and micro) of initial conditions. The macro-level conditions include “different traditions for stakeholder involvement in different countries and in different parts of the public sector” (p. 106). At the meso level, collaborative innovation is influenced by “different legal and institutional conditions for participatory governance in different policy fields” (p. 106). The micro-level conditions indicate asymmetries of power, resource and knowledge, past experiences with cooperation or conflict, and incentives for participation (Ansell and Gash 2008). As a main component of collaborative innovation theory, institutional arenas of interaction consist of three subcomponents: triggers of collaborative innovation, collaborative innovation processes, and drivers and barriers. Torfing suggests push or pull factors as the triggers of collaborative collaboration. Push factors pertain to a situation where state and nonstate stakeholders “seek to escape the present predicament, or … that is perceived to be unsustainable due to the emergence or aggravation of some serious problems” (p. 113). Pull factors are at work when state and nonstate stakeholders face positive and ambitious challenges that urge them to pursue a new and attractive direction or when we exploit new opportunities generating new and desirable things. But he notes that those pull or push factors act as “a necessary but insufficient condition for initiating public innovation processes” (p. 117). He focuses on the role of social and political entrepreneurs who problematize existing practices and construct new opportunities to develop innovative solutions. Next, Torfing conducts in-depth analysis on the different aspects of collaborative innovation processes. First, he categorizes actors of collaborative innovation processes into three types: the affected actors (those who are directly influenced by particular problems and solutions for the problems); relevant actors (those who have experience, knowledge, expertise in creating, implementing, and diffusing novel solutions); and intermediaries and boundary spanners (those who are capable of facilitating actors to share their expertise, skills, and resources with others). Mobilizing and empowering actors who have diverse and applicable assets is essential for designing and implementing innovative solutions in an institutional arena of interaction. Torfing views collaborative innovation processes as collective learning. Innovative solutions “are usually a product of learning that is stimulated by the exchange of information, views, and ideas between multiple actors with different knowledge bases and forms of expertise” (p. 180). Collaborative learning can be achieved through collective discourse by comparing and assessing the reflections of multiple actors. Especially, he introduces emerging literature on user-driven or citizen-centered innovation. From this perspective, citizens’ experiences and ideas are an important resource for producing novel public solutions. Thus, citizens are considered as proactive co-creators of innovative solutions instead of passive customers of public service. He also identifies and describes key obstacles that hinder the decision and implementation of innovative solutions. These obstacles include uncertainty about the appropriateness and impacts of solutions, probable risks, complexity caused by the involvement of multiple actors, collective action problems (prisoner’s dilemmas and free riding), and power struggles and conflicts. Torfing stresses that traditional rationalistic approaches (cost-benefit analysis and public discourse based on communicative rationality) are unlikely to address such obstacles in collaborative innovation processes. Instead, to select and implement innovative solutions, “deliberative processes must combine the accumulation of arguments based on reason with the articulation of a hegemonic discourse that is capable of mobilizing passion and constructing visions” (p. 207). Thus, he contends that conflicts and power struggles can facilitate multiple actors to pursue intelligent change in institutional arenas of interaction. Also from a practical point of view, it is important to connect the selection and implementation of innovative solutions to the daily operations of public organizations, for example, by integrating frontline personnel’s experiences and skills and competent knowledge workers’ expertise to initiate and manage collaborative innovation processes. Another important topic that needs to be considered regarding collaborative innovation processes is the diffusion of public innovation. Rogers (1995)’s innovation diffusion model consisting of five stages (knowledge, persuasion, decision, implementation, and confirmation) is utilized to analyze how innovative solutions are diffused through collaborative networks. According to this model, innovation diffusion facilitates dynamic communication between suppliers of policy innovation and potential adopters and their communication “is often mediated by change agents and opinion leaders” (p. 304). Also, an organizational learning approach is emphasized to understand the impact and role of governance networks on innovation diffusion. From this perspective, innovation diffusion in governance networks is a result of a mix of the internal search for new ideas and external opportunities and knowledge. The third subcomponent of institutional arenas of interaction is drivers of and barriers to collaborative innovation in the public sector. Torfing focuses on the four types of the drivers of collaborative innovation. An important driver of innovation is problems, challenges, and opportunities identified as “public.” Those problems, challenges, and opportunities likely spur “a moral obligation to participate in processes of collaborative problem solving” (p. 239). The second driver is that public organizations are embedded in the same overall rules, norms, and values. He considers citizen engagement in policy decision making and implementation as a crucial driver of innovation. Citizen engagement oftentimes not only enables citizens to make their voices heard in the policy decision making and implementation process, but also enhances the collaborative capacity of the public sector. Torfing categorizes various barriers to collaborative innovation into three types: barriers to interaction acting as a precondition of collaboration, barriers to collaboration acting as a precondition of innovation, and barriers to innovation. The barriers to interaction include the lack of necessity or urgency regarding social problems and challenges, the absence of a tradition for interaction in the policy area, negative previous experiences with participatory and interactive decision making, and weak political support. He suggests as the barriers to collaboration large power asymmetries, a competitive environment, and opportunistic behavior. The barriers to innovation indicate the lack of diversity of worldviews, the presence of veto players blocking the group’s ability to collaborate, political complexity, and operational uncertainty. Crucially, Torfing contends that public leaders and mangers can help overcome the barriers by playing the role of conveners, facilitators, and catalysts. To address the barriers to interaction, they are required to become the convener that “brings together the relevant and affected actors and … triggers an initial exchange of information, views, and ideas” (p. 245). They also can serve as the facilitator for collaboration by managing internal differences between actors and creating mutual learning. Public leaders and managers as the catalyst need “to create appropriate disturbances and encourage the actors to think outside the box and use their different competences and capacities to develop and implement new and bold solutions” (p. 246). Torfing finally emphasizes that the roles of the convener, the facilitator, and the catalyst are based on new forms of leadership, including adaptive leadership, distributive (or horizontal) leadership, and collaborative leadership. Undoubtedly, I believe that this book and collaborative innovation theory in particular makes a significant theoretical contribution to the literature on governance networks and innovation that have been previously disconnected. Collaborative innovation theory can “help us ask some good and relevant research questions, conceptualize and categorize the main determinants in processes of collaborative innovation, and understand network-based collaboration and innovation processes” (p. 75). This book can be also useful for practitioners to understand collaborative innovation processes and to develop their own leadership and management strategies for designing and implementing innovative solutions in the public sector. However, as Torfing mentioned, collaborative innovation theory (and 41 propositions articulated in the book) calls for the further development and modification of the theory based on empirical testing. In particular, I want to emphasize two things for future research. First, collaborative innovation may not be an ultimate goal that state and nonstate stakeholders collectively pursue. In other words, multiple actors participate in designing and implementing innovative solutions to generate specific social, economic, or political benefits to individuals, organizations, or the community at large. Thus, potentially, collaborative innovation theory may need to be extended by considering its various impacts and benefits. In this regard, the public value framework can be useful (Moore 1995). This perspective takes into account a wide range of substantive (economic, political, social, strategic, and quality of life) and intrinsic (ideological and perceptional) benefits and impacts that public administration and policy can create. From this perspective, collaborative innovation may be viewed as a “value-generating mechanism” instead of a final goal and outcome (Harrison et al. 2012). Next, I note that nonstate stakeholders—including the general public, nonprofit organizations, and for-profit corporations—are currently developing and implementing collaborative innovations in diverse policy sectors (emergency preparedness and response, environmental protection, human and social services, international development, etc.). For example, in recent disaster and crisis situations, nonstate stakeholders proactively processed a large amount of disaster and crisis data from multiple sources and collaborated with government agencies to coordinate rescue missions and the delivery of aid resources in a timely and efficient manner (Park and Johnston 2017). From this perspective, nonstate stakeholders are not just “invited” collaborators. They oftentimes act as the initiators and designers of governance networks for collaborative innovation. But, it seems that collaborative innovation theory developed by Torfing focuses more attention on the role of state stakeholders than that of nonstate stakeholders. Thus, scholars may need to conduct more studies on nonstate stakeholder-driven innovation.

t: The State of Federal Inspectors General Studies
abs: When a scholar is the first to study a particular social scientific phenomenon in depth, his or her thoughts shape future scholarship for some time. Such is case with Light (1993) and his examination of federal offices of inspector general (OIGs) in Monitoring Government: Inspectors General and the Search for Accountability (1993). In this seminal book, Light explored the adoption of the federal Inspectors General Act of 1978 and the development of the OIG institution as it expanded across the federal government. Light covered a wide swath of ground in his study of OIGs and arrived at a fairly disheartening conclusion for the OIGs role in government accountability that there are multiple incentives and pressures in place to encourage OIGs to pursue compliance-oriented reviews of the agencies they oversee and eschew more difficult capacity-building initiatives. Two recent books, including the one by Hilliard that is the subject of this book review, respond to Light’s critique. Apaza (2013) provides a straightforward defense of the OIG system with a case study of the Department of Homeland Security OIG and argues that OIGs do in fact take on more complicated capacity-related reviews. Hilliard, however, crafts a more creative counternarrative to Light’s analysis by employing a democratic legitimacy lens. Through a qualitative study, she argues that OIGs have a role in contributing to important democratic principles, especially in times of national emergency. In other words, OIGs are not constrained to fostering accountability through compliance reviews, but can contribute to much loftier ideals. Yet she notes that OIGs’ success in doing so varies widely. She explains, “My goal is neither to test nor build a comprehensive theory of a systematic mechanism. Rather it is to explain a particular historical outcome, a single-outcome study: the success and differential development of a monitory body in forging different modes of democratic practice” (p. 39). In pursuit of her goal, Hilliard picks up where Light left off, historically speaking. She closely examines the creation, evolution, and work of the OIGs of the State Department, the Department of Justice, and the Department of Homeland Security, all of which were created long after the federal IG Act of 1978 was adopted. She demonstrates that in the course of pursuing fraud, waste, and abuse and promoting effectiveness and efficiency, OIGs have a role that Light may have overlooked: the ability to promote democratic debate by keeping citizens, their representatives, and civil society organizations appraised of the goings-on in federal agencies. This role can invoke debate about constitutional rights, bureaucratic ethics, and appropriate limits to the executive function. Yet, Hilliard finds that OIGs are not always fulfilling this democratic function. She uses the experiences of the OIGs at the Departments of State, Justice, and Homeland Security to show how varying leadership and management decisions shape the extent to which an OIG can encourage democratic values. Through an incredibly detailed history of these federal OIGs, Hilliard develops three types of OIG contributions to democracy: a political democracy at State; a constitutional democracy at Justice; and a managerial democracy at Homeland Security. Hilliard demonstrates how the State Department OIG reacted to the overcharged political landscape, which inhibited its ability to contribute to the democratic narrative. On the other hand, the Justice OIG, with its staff of attorneys, addressed issues of civil rights, not through the language of rights, but through its focus on administrative procedure and underspecified laws. This approach encouraged debate on constitutional issues in Congress and in other venues. The Homeland Security OIG, overseeing an agency that was hastily created in a time of national emergency, focused on the management of government during times of crises. As a result, a larger democratic debate arose about the extent to which government procedures should be loosened to respond to such emergencies. In her recounting, Hilliard shows that OIGs are not simply inhibited by institutional constraints or legislative mandates, albeit these issues shape OIG activities. She argues that OIGs are also capable of contributing to higher ideals than simply catching fraudsters or identifying waste. OIGs are cast in a near heroic light in the text, which could be an inspiring message to accountability advocates and practitioners alike. For example, Hilliard states, “With the latitude [OIGs] have to choose which actions are worthy of being investigated, and [the ability] to select the terms in which to narrate them, the IGs set the moral and ethical standards by which the government must then act” (p. 14). In fact, one might wonder if Hilliard is proposing a new way to assess OIGs’ effectiveness. Yet, an important normative issue arises from this text. Should OIGs aspire to contribute to these democratic ideals? Should OIGs assess the constitutionality of agency actions? Should OIGs weigh in on civil rights violations? Should OIGs rule on the legality of agency actions? Should OIGs push agencies to act ethically and not just legally? Although Hilliard makes a strong case that there is a role for OIGs in contributing to democratic debate beyond simple monitoring, other scholars who argue against increased government accountability as an onerous constraint on public managers might disagree (e.g., Behn 2001). Beyond the role of OIGs in democracy, Hilliard also sends a more subtle message that an OIG’s role, whether contributing to the traditional notion of government accountability or the higher goal of shoring up democratic principles, is very fragile. Hilliard’s histories emphasize that OIGs do not work in a vacuum and are beset with multiple challenges that are out of their control, from limited resources, criticism from their agencies and Congress, pre-existing bureaucratic structures, competing legislative mandates, and shifting national priorities. Further, problems internal to the OIG such as unstable leadership, poor quality training, less than rigorous reviews, or inaccurate conclusions undermine the OIGs’ role. Hilliard’s narrative also highlights the tenuous ability of OIGs to make real change and hold people accountable without external actors taking the lead through other parallel processes of accountability. Hilliard raises these issues but does not analyze them. Perhaps Hilliard’s approach makes sense because of her focus on democratic legitimacy and the paucity of research on federal OIGs from which to build. Nevertheless, these other issues certainly deserve the attention of scholars. Hilliard certainly writes for an academic audience. The text contains vaulted language, dense prose, and complex concepts. As a result, the text is not easily accessible to practitioners. This represents a lost opportunity. Current Inspectors General could learn much about how OIGs might contribute to a larger democratic debate while also safeguarding their independence, which is essential to their role as monitors. I fear the text is challenging to the layperson, and thus, the larger implications for policy and practice may be inaccessible. In summary, Hilliard elevates the institution of an OIG. OIGs are not mere instruments of legal compliance and monitoring, but have the potential to be important contributors in the pursuit of democratic ideals. While the other more traditional roles of OIGs in monitoring for fraud, waste, and abuse and completing financial and performance audit should not be diminished, this book, with its unique approach, is a welcome addition. Hilliard provides a close look at an important institution in modern US government that continues to evolve. Hilliard’s work has the potential to reinvigorate theoretical work on the topic of government accountability through bureaucratic structures like the OIGs.

t: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty under Municipal Decline: A Difference-in-Differences Analysis in Japan
abs: Drawing on Albert Hirschman’s Exit, Voice, and Loyalty, this study aims to reveal citizens’ response mechanisms to the decline of municipality caused by municipal management failure. Using the case of the Japanese town Ohwani in fiscal crisis, this study examines the effects of fiscal reform, which involve tax increases, service cuts, and political conflicts, on citizens’ exit intention and voice activities. For this purpose, this study makes a quasi-experimental framework that contrasts Ohwani to Inakadate, a control village not under fiscal reform which has similar socio-demographic features. The estimation approach is a difference-in-differences design with a time difference enabled by a careful retrospective measurement. Data were collected from 600 randomly sampled citizens of Ohwani and Inakadate with a response rate of 45%. This study finds that citizens under fiscal reform are more likely to consider exit, while the level of citizens’ voice activities is unaffected by fiscal reform. In addition, social capital factors show a loyalty function that encourages voice activities as the covariates, though those associations with exit intention are weak. This study provides initial evidence for citizens’ response mechanisms to municipal decline and identifies keys to successful recuperation from decline.

t: Understanding Individual and Organizational Level Representation: The Case of Parental Involvement in Schools
abs: With the substantive effects of racial and ethnic representation well-documented in the representative bureaucracy literature, scholars have increasingly turned their attention to better understanding the causal mechanisms underlying these effects. One explored but yet unresolved issue is whether the benefits of representation stem from individual (direct)- versus organizational (indirect)-level pathways, or both. The current study advances this conversation by testing the effect of both levels of representation on parental involvement in schools using a current, nationally-representative dataset: the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study, Kindergarten Class of 2010–2011 (ECLS-K: 2011). In doing so, this study also contributes to research on parental involvement, and how it may relate to racial and ethnic achievement gaps. Results indicate that both direct and indirect representation matter, though perhaps not equally. Direct representation has a larger association with parental involvement outcomes, especially for nonwhite students. After controlling for this direct representation, indirect representation shows statistically significant but smaller increases in parent-reported conference attendance.

t: A Great Place to Start
abs: What kind of subject is public management/public administration? That is the central question of Christopher Pollitt’s Advanced Introduction to Public Management and Administration. In addressing the question, Pollitt describes “the ideas, methods, people and institutions which comprise contemporary academic public management and administration” (p. 3) as he guides readers through many of the key aspects and issues central to the field. Though Pollitt acknowledges there are some advantages and disadvantages to adopting this type of broad frame, by the end of the text, he masterfully narrates the field of public management in a concise and easily digestible way. This contribution will aid his primary audience—graduate students and junior scholars interested in public management—develop a foundation upon which to build their research. Although this book should not be considered unitarily sufficient as an introduction to the field, it should become a necessary compliment to the collection of readings often prescribed to gain a foundational understanding of public management. For example, in addition to the canon of public management literature, it might fit nicely with Henry’s (1975) “Paradigms of Public Administration” or Riccucci’s (2010)Public Administration: Traditions of Inquiry and Philosophies of Knowledge. Senior scholars may also find some value in his work, especially as a compendium to their teaching. Chapters 2 (theory) and 3 (methods and approaches) cover key aspects of public management. Although admittedly lengthy, these chapters provide a high-quality overview of the basics of public management scholarship as it stands today. In addition to three “big name” theories—neo-institutionalism, rational choice theory, and governance theory—in Chapter 2, Pollitt also spends some time discussing theories that are smaller in scope or only of salience to public management scholars. Chapter 3 covers a wide range of qualitative and quantitative methods and tools incorporated by public management scholars in their research. Pollitt discusses some problems for public management related to the philosophy of science and encourages readers to be more deliberate about the claims surrounding research and the philosophical approaches used to get there (see also Raadschelders 2011). The contents of these chapters are essential in any review of public management and presenting and distilling such a broad literature is challenging. However, more could be done to help those with little exposure to the discipline think about how they might incorporate Pollitt’s suggestions into their research or how they might generally think about orienting themselves to a particular theory or methodological approach. Chapter 4 addresses an unusual topic for a review piece—the public management community. I thought describing the public management diaspora as, “the community of men and women and organizations that make up the discipline or field” (p. 100) was a welcome and informative change from most reviews. By incorporating a more anthropological or cultural perspective, Pollitt can sensitize newcomers to “what kind of family they are getting themselves into” (p. 100). This is an amenable approach because it is a different way to present information about the field, and it speaks to some experiences I have had during my short tenure as a public management scholar. Although the chapters about methods and theories are centered on the tools public administration scholars use, this section is used by Pollitt to describe the people who use those tools and explain why they use them. He also argues that the internationalization of public management scholarship in recent decades is an important phenomenon to understand. Speaking as an Englishman and primarily from the perspective of the Anglophone world of public management, Pollitt recognizes that most come to public management interested in understanding problems and questions which arise from their own domestic context. At the same time, he argues the contributions and collaborations of scholars from around the world serve to strengthen the field. In Chapter 5, Pollitt asks the reader-scholar to think outward—that is, to think about the implications of public management beyond a strictly academic endeavor. His orientation could be characterized by saying that because of its “distinctive relationship to practice and practitioners” (p. 4), most public management scholars should strive to balance both academic and practical interests. Thus, he advocates for finding a balance between practical and academic work such that scholars will want to get involved in bridge-building with practitioners or, at a minimum, become interested in communicating the applied implications of their research. There were two parts of Pollitt’s argument at this point in the text that seemed overly simple, especially for someone just starting out in the field. First, a junior researcher’s desire to develop practitioner relationships might push against the incentives in academia that shape the career trajectory of a junior scholar. Pollitt does not talk about how junior scholars might navigate this tension. Second, Pollitt suggests practitioners want academic advice and offers some ways in which working with academics can benefit practitioners. Still, practitioners and scholars will often have different objectives they are trying to achieve, which raises questions about the stability of a long-term partnership. Thus, what we often get is encouragement to devote time and resources to practitioners but a “tendency for the academic ivory tower to stand further and further away” from the realities of managing government (p. 114). The goal which Pollitt would have us aim to achieve from a reading of this chapter seems like it might be impractical for most early career scholars. Another approach could be to discuss how scholars might successfully incorporate practitioner interactions into their research agenda early in their careers. This problem could different outside the United States if public management scholars in other countries enjoy a public-sector which has greater support of scientific endeavors than in the United States. Nonetheless, what seems missing from this work is a better discussion of the implications of thinking about public management as a design science, as a pure scientific discipline, or as a field within another social science discipline. Pollitt’s book does not prompt the reader to think about how one orients their research efforts towards one of these labels or another. Instead, he tries to communicate the importance of having at least some orientation towards practice. In other words, we cannot study public management without having a concern for the way it works in the real world. Chapter 6 discusses current and future megatrends which should be of interest to public management scholars. These issues include changes in climate, demographics, and technology as well as recent attempts at fiscal austerity. By thinking about these megatrends now, and by considering how they might become wicked problems, public management scholars can apply their knowledge in a way that would benefit society in a meaningful way. As a current doctoral candidate, my primary takeaway from reading the text is that I wish this resource was available to me when I started learning about public management scholarship. In fact, it may even be a great place to start a doctoral education in public management. At the same time, there is so much material here that graduate students could get lost or at least miss key points without an advisor or instructor to guide them through discussions and questions which build from the text. Although the book does a great job of laying out the space, a senior scholar can provide extra context to the questions and tensions Pollitt raises in this very useful book.

t: Antipolitics and the Hindrance of Performance Management in Education
abs: Performance management reforms are a popular way to try to create responsive and improving government. These types of reforms have become commonplace in education policy and the Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory (JPART) has been one of the leading venues for research on these topics. However, under-analyzed are the ways in which performance management policies represent antipolitical bent to education reform. We outline an argument that avoiding political decisionmaking in favor of reforms that create authoritative or purportedly neutral data risks undertaking policy change are not as meaningful as hoped. We select eight articles that represent research on performance management broadly and are thought provoking for a broader consideration of performance management in education policy.

t: Collaborative Platforms as a Governance Strategy
abs: Collaborative governance is increasingly viewed as a proactive policy instrument, one in which the strategy of collaboration can be deployed on a larger scale and extended from one local context to another. This article suggests that the concept of collaborative platforms provides useful insights into this strategy of treating collaborative governance as a generic policy instrument. Building on an organization-theoretic approach, collaborative platforms are defined as organizations or programs with dedicated competences and resources for facilitating the creation, adaptation and success of multiple or ongoing collaborative projects or networks. Working between the theoretical literature on platforms and empirical cases of collaborative platforms, the article finds that strategic intermediation and design rules are important for encouraging the positive feedback effects that help collaborative platforms adapt and succeed. Collaborative platforms often promote the scaling-up of collaborative governance by creating modular collaborative units—a strategy of collaborative franchising.

t: Improving Governance of Risk and Uncertainty
abs: As author Mark Matthews notes in the afterword, this book represents a “formative stage in a longer-term project” (190) and, as such, there is much here to commend. Scholars of risk and public policy have long noted that governments are often ineffective risk managers. Governments are thought to under-react or over-react to risk partly because of democratic accountability. Given that the risk perceptions of the public frequently diverge from those of scientists and technical experts, government responsiveness to the public leads to poor risk management and an increased potential for, what Matthews terms, “nasty surprises.” Additionally, problems may be poorly understood and, as a result, policies may have unintended consequences. Finally, certain types of uncertainty are compounded by the vast amounts of information that confront policymakers, coupled with their limited ability to attend to all the potentially important pieces of information. In this book, Matthews offers a new diagnosis of the problematic ways that governments handle information and uncertainty as well as some solutions. Matthews argues that a focus on New Public Management (NPM), evidence-based policymaking, and compliance rituals by government agencies impedes learning in the face of risk and uncertainty. NPM brought on changes in thinking about how governments should perform their duties as well as the types of things for which governments should be accountable. Most problematic for Matthews is the reliance on performance-based metrics through which government success is measured. As a result, government accountability is based on meeting certain performance metrics, regardless of whether there are improvements in the underlying problems that governments are addressing. In addition, a focus on evidence, or “fact” based policymaking has led to academic debates regarding data quality and analytical rigor that are typically far too technical for decision-makers. Finally, compliance rituals are problematic because the focus is on satisfying certain bureaucratic routines and procedures rather than attending to other potentially important types of information. Because of these factors, governments are constrained in how they think about and respond to risk. The rigid focus on output metrics, evidence produced in an increasing technical fashion, and reliance on bureaucratic routines limits a government’s ability to adapt to changing circumstances. The book puts forth new and interesting ways to think about governance in a world filled with risk, uncertainty, and the potential for nasty surprises. Matthews argues that governance should aim to make nasty surprises less likely, yet current governance practices are not optimal for achieving that objective and may, in fact, make some surprises more likely. To illustrate this potential Matthews develops a heuristic he terms the “risk amplification ratio,” which is the proportion of “achieved potential for surprise” to the “unavoidable potential for surprise” (p.112). Risks tend to be amplified by government entropy, which reduces the ability of governments to anticipate and effectively respond to events. Government entropy is defined as the difference between the achieved potential for surprise and the unavoidable potential for surprise and is an “expression of the well-understood tendency for bureaucracies to [self-organize] around internal interests and incentives rather than generate public value outside of governance” (p.113). For Matthews, entropy is a way to understand information and uncertainty and is useful for both diagnosing the problem as well as providing ways to address the tendency of governments to miss weak information signals, thereby increasing the potential for nasty surprises. Apart from the risk amplification ratio and government entropy, Matthews also notes that Bayesian inference can be used to improve the capacity of governments to mitigate uncertainty and risk. According to Matthews, governments could better detect and process information signals and uncertainty using Bayesian inference, as opposed to the more commonly used frequentist approach. Matthews describes the difference in the following way: To a Bayesian, the concept of probability refers to the state of knowledge, expressed in terms of the degree to which different competing hypotheses may be correct given the available evidence. To a classical statistician, probability refers to the observed frequency of different events. In other words, one definition of probability refers to hypotheses given available data and the other, data independent of hypotheses (p.97). The approach of the classical statisticians, or frequentists, is to assume that information is acquired and uncertainty reduced only when we can be reasonably confident, typically with a probability less than .05, that the observed data were not generated by a random process. This approach works well for hypothesis testing in a scientific experiment, where it is applied to test the probability of an observed outcome relative to a null hypothesis. However, Matthews argues that the frequentist approach may not be as useful in the dynamic process of policy related decision-making, where policy changes are intended to alter behavior. Bayesian analysis however, offers a way to update information during policy development and decision-making. In brief, Bayesian inference is based on conditional probabilities, where beliefs, expressed as odds associated with a testable hypothesis, are updated conditional on prior beliefs and new information. Therefore, as Matthews notes, “we are able to update the assumed odds of something happening when new information is obtained” (p. 99). An additional advantage of Bayesian inference is that its odds-based approach is more naturally intuitive than the “decimal probabilities” that are typically associated with classical statistics. Combining both signal processing and Bayesian inference, Matthews argues that, to reduce the likelihood of nasty surprises, governments should use policy interventions as binary (true/false positive, true/false negative) hypotheses tests. For this to work, policy interventions would need to be structured as a series of binary hypotheses regarding the impact of the specific interventions on specific outcomes. The hypotheses to be tested would be determined by the relevant stakeholders, and the hypotheses would be tested through Bayesian inference. A major advantage of this approach is that it encourages learning-by-doing through consistent updating as new information becomes available regarding the evidence for each hypothesis. This consistent updating makes the detection of weak signals more likely, thereby decreasing the likelihood of nasty surprises. An additional advantage is that hypothesis testing throughout the life of a policy or project can integrate ex ante formulation, the implementation process, and ex post evaluation. Finally, this approach would examine what is arguably most important—the impact of specific policy interventions on outcomes—as opposed to current practices of measuring desired performance metrics, which may or may not be decisive in determining the effectiveness of the policy. As Matthews argues, his approach would move learning from simply the compliance rituals of current governance practice to an integrated process of continual appraisal, evaluation, and risk management. As noted, there is much to commend in this book, particularly the criticisms of the ways in which current governance structures may lend themselves to an increased propensity to experience unexpected events. It is certainly hard to argue with the sentiment that, as Matthews states, public policy should strive to be an “iterative process of investing in increasing the odds of things occurring that we want to occur and decreasing the odds of things occurring that we don’t want to take place” (163). In addition, in a world of “alternative facts” designing systems that facilitate learning and information use by policymakers is critical, and Matthews has put forth important ideas that merit careful consideration by academics, practitioners, and policy makers. There are a few factors however, that make implementation of some of the ideas presented difficult. First is the technical capacity needed to perform the analysis that Matthews recommends. Although Bayesian inference is perhaps more intuitive to understand than frequentist inference, Bayesian analysis is a technical and somewhat complex undertaking, which might make it difficult to convince practitioners and policymakers to adopt it as an approach. A second concern is the inertia of the various organizations that would need to collaborate for the approach proposed to be successful. For example, Matthews argues that academia should be involved in the technical aspects of reviewing evidence and civil society organizations should be involved in the development of hypotheses to test. However, divisions of labor between government, academic, and civil society organizations have led to the development of different methodologies and specializations that make integration of the information generating and processing elements of these organizations difficult. In addition, academia does not currently recognize for tenure and promotion purposes the type of applied and review work that academics would need to perform within the framework proposed by Matthews. Finally, current government practices are path dependent and a result of previous decisions, laws, and rules. Therefore, much of what governments do are bound by precedents and law, which limits the ability of governments to innovate. Overall, I think Matthews has offered scholars of public policy and public administration a book that deserves to be read and considered carefully. I look forward to seeing how the longer term project develops, and I expect other scholars will as well.

t: Public Service Sector: The Compassionate Workplace—The Effect of Compassion and Stress on Employee Engagement, Burnout, and Performance
abs: This study seeks to investigate the effect of compassion in the public service workplace. Our compassion model is based on public service sector employees who receive compassionate feelings such as affection, generosity, caring, and tenderness from their supervisors. A longitudinal study of 166 public service employees, their supervisors and 333 of their clients (citizens) was conducted in Israel. In this longitudinal study, we found evidence that receipt of compassion from supervisors (at time 1) in the public service workplace was positively associated with employees' sense of work engagement, and negatively related to their work burnout (at time 2). Furthermore, receipt of compassion (at time 1) was also found to impact public service employees' organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) and knowledge sharing (at time 2) as rated by their supervisors, as well as their service-oriented performance of compassionate behavior toward clients (at time 2), rated by the citizens. Finally, we found evidence for compassion acting as a mechanism for coping with common stressful public service conditions such as demanding citizens and administrative workload, which are inherent in this sector. Compassion in the public service workplace may therefore be salient in effecting public service work performance, and as such should be consciously targeted by public sector managers and policy makers.

t: Children of a Lesser God: Administrative Burden and Social Equity in Citizen–State Interactions
abs: An important research agenda in public administration is to investigate how formal and realized public policy influences the lives of marginalized social groups. Recently, reinvigorated research on administrative burden can make useful contributions to this line of inquiry. Using ethnographic research methods, this article analyzes administrative burden experienced by the Khawaja Sira—individuals culturally defined as neither men nor women—of Pakistan in getting a legal ID. In doing so, this article contributes to a better understanding of the role played by third parties, administrative behavior and social factors play in influencing the level of administrative burden and social inequity for genderqueer groups.

t: Picking the Team: A Preliminary Experimental Study of the Activation of Collaborative Network Members
abs: Among a collaborative leader’s most important duties is selecting a collaborative partner. Numerous perspectives, including resource dependency theory, institutional theory, transaction cost theory, and personality typologies, have been used to help explain this decision. Clearly, a collaborative leader would desire to work with an individual who has access to needed resources, has a personality that fits the network, and is familiar. However, such a perfect partner does not often, if ever, exist. Therefore, a collaborative leader must make trade-offs between the issues of resource access, personality, and familiarity. Using an experimental design, this study explores how collaborative leaders make these trade-offs when considering potential collaborative partners. The findings suggest that while prospective partner personality may be the most significant driver of the partnership decision, it is actually the combination of factors, especially personality and resource access that interact to determine partner desirability.

t: The Liaison Office for Personnel Management and Its Role in Shaping Federal Human Resource Management
abs: Mordecai Lee’s A Presidential Civil Service stands out as a substantive contribution to the field of public administration’s historical understanding of the nation’s current civil service system and its “executive-centric” approach to managing career federal employees (p. 6). By focusing his analysis on the often overlooked history and significance of the Liaison Office for Personnel Management (LOPM), which operated from 1939 to 1953, Lee highlights the early development of the presidential paradigm of executive branch management, a paradigm where the civil service workforce is governed by a presidentially appointed executive, as well as lower level appointees, focused on responsiveness and the “ability to manage” as opposed to an independent civil service commission with a near singular focus on merit-based appointments and political neutrality. For contemporary students of public administration, and federal human resource management in particular, the period between the passage of the Pendleton Act of 1883 to the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 is often provided only cursory attention, with many textbook narratives simply highlighting the culminating need for greater management flexibility as the driving force behind the creation of the US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and Merit Systems Protection Board. In line with the historical research of such scholars as Van Riper (1958) and White (2008), Lee seeks to provide a more robust understanding of the conceptual and practical underpinnings of current federal human resource management policy by providing a very detailed analysis of development, activities, and dissolution of the LOPM. Overall, this is an extremely well-written and engaging text, especially considering its focus on what, at first glance, could be considered by some to be a relatively inconsequential artifact of public administration history. Though many may consider it a historical footnote in the management of federal personnel, the LOPM was created by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1939 following recommendations made by the Brownlow Committee, which advocated for the establishment of a presidential personnel administrator. FDR’s establishment of the LOPM, as Lee successfully makes the case, was highly significant in that it marked one of the first shifts from a progressive era emphasis on merit through the governance of the Civil Service Commission to the beginnings of a push for presidentially driven management, an effort that would fully manifest itself years later through the establishment of the US OPM in 1978. Lee outlines four primary rationales for undertaking such an exhaustive study of the LOPM. First, the establishment of the LOPM can be viewed as the definitive point in which the paradigm of presidential management of the civil service, as opposed to complete control by the Civil Service Commission, took root. Second, the establishment of the LOPM could also be viewed as part of a larger battle over the proper balance of power between Congress and the Executive Branch. Third, the careful analysis of the history of the LOPM builds upon the larger body of historical research on the foundations of public administration in the United States, a focus that Lee points out has been advocated by leading public administration scholars. Fourth, assessing the failure of the LOPM to permanently shape federal management under FDR still provides a valuable framework for understanding later reform efforts. In terms of structure, A Presidential Civil Service is organized into six chronological chapters beginning with the period leading up to the creation of the LOPM, its founding and development from 1939 through 1953, and the period between the dissolution of LOPM and the later formation of the OPM. While the text contains the level of detail one would expect from such a historical review, it is very well written and would be well suited for those with an interest in US government history, public administration and, most importantly, those seeking a deeper understanding of our current system for managing federal personnel. In addition to providing an exhaustive overview of the LOPM, one of the more delightful contributions of the text is its extensive focus on the LOPM’s founding Administrative Assistant (i.e., Director), William H. McReynolds. While the careers of civil servants are often overlooked in the historical overviews of public administration, Lee’s detailed analysis of McReynolds’ efforts within the LOPM stands out as a noteworthy exception. With regards to the text’s contemporary relevance, Lee’s focus on the historical role of the LOPM and development of a management-centric approach to governing the executive branch also highlights the irony in President Donald J. Trump’s implicit decision to leave many of the executive branch presidential appointments unfilled, including the Director of the OPM. In contrast to decades of presidential transition efforts to quickly relieve career civil servants serving on an interim basis during a transition in leadership, President Trump, for reasons that are not entirely clear, has elected to leave many of these individuals in place, thus returning, in no small part, to a paradigm of merit as opposed to the “executive-centric” management we have come to expect since 1978. While A Presidential Civil Service will serve as a worthwhile addition to survey courses in public administration and, in particular, public human resource management, my sole criticism of the text is the author’s framing of the transition from the US Civil Service Commission to the US OPM as a shift in focus from merit to management. While I appreciate the nuances of this framework, it could also be misleading to many new students of public administration who are not fully aware of the current system’s relatively robust focus on merit via such mechanisms as the Merit Systems Principals and Prohibited Personnel Practices. Although it is true that contemporary presidents possess a greater ability to manage federal agencies under the executive leadership of the OPM, it is also the case that the roughly 1.8 million federal employees hired through merit-based selection processes still represent the heart and soul of the modern civil service system, even in the absence of the Civil Service Commission. Most importantly, it is this continued and sustained focus on merit which can ultimately insulate the country from the ills of presidential administrations either unfit or unwilling to manage the civil service.

t: Compared to What? How Social and Historical Reference Points Affect Citizens’ Performance Evaluations
abs: The question of what is “good” or “poor” performance is difficult to answer without applying a reference point—a standard for comparison. Citizens’ evaluation of performance information will, therefore, tend to be guided by reference points. We test how reference points alter citizens’ evaluation of organizational performance. In this article, drawing on Herbert Simon, we test how citizens use historical (internal) and social (external) reference points when making relative comparisons: how important is current performance relative to past performance? And how important is current performance relative to the performance of other organizations? Two experiments are embedded within a large nationally representative sample of citizens (n = 3,443). The experiments assign historical and social reference points for performance data on education and unemployment to citizens. We find that citizens’ performance evaluation is fundamentally a relative process. Interestingly, we show that social reference points are almost twice as important in citizens’ evaluations as historical reference points. We find some evidence of a negativity bias in citizens’ relative evaluations. The strong social reference point effects have implications for studying citizens’ response to performance and how managers can frame and manipulate external performance data.

t: Administrative Centralization and Bureaucratic Responsiveness: Evidence from the Food Stamp Program
abs: Delegation of administrative authority is commonly thought to involve a tradeoff between the discretion necessary for bureaucratic effectiveness and democratic responsiveness. In many contexts, however, discretion and responsiveness go hand-in-hand: Street-level bureaucrats may adapt their behavior to accommodate local norms and values, even when implementing the identical statutory language. I argue that this type of bureaucratic adaptation can explain local variation in participation rates in the national food stamp program. By exploiting between-state differences in the level at which the program is administered, I further show that administrative centralization does not appear to moderate such responsiveness, which is high across institutional settings. Using data on application denial rates for a subset of these states, I offer additional evidence that some of the county-level variation in program participation is a product of decisions made by local caseworkers. Together, these findings offer important insights on the institutional preconditions for bureaucratic responsiveness and control.

t: The Impact of Administrative Structure on the Ability of City Governments to Overcome Functional Collective Action Dilemmas: A Climate and Energy Perspective
abs: Fragmented authority and service responsibilities within governments can impact the design and implementation of policy.
