Administrative structures can play an important role in mitigating the challenges associated with coordinating activities across independent units within city government. In this study, we use the broad policy arena of sustainability as a testbed to explore “Functional Collective Action” problems and the consequences of cities’ administrative design on the portfolio of policy actions related to energy and climate protection. Empirical analyses of survey data from a national sample of local governments indicate that political institutions, government capacity, and community support influence, to varying degrees, administrative structures related to sustainability initiatives. Our analyses also suggest that these are not inconsequential decisions, since they influence the extent to which cities achieve greater policy integration.

t: Does Benchmarking Encourage Improvement or Convergence? Evaluating North Carolina’s Fiscal Benchmarking Tool
abs: Several states monitor the fiscal health of their local governments by “benchmarking” them—using a suite of financial indicators to track performance over time. Benchmarking of public organizations can facilitate performance management, leading to the spread of best practices and improved organizational performance. It is also possible that benchmarking, absent other performance routines, could create isomorphic pressures that encourage local governments to adopt policies that converge performance or financial indicators towards the group mean. This article tests these hypotheses using the introduction of North Carolina’s financial benchmarking tool in 2010. We construct a panel of the 14 indicators used to assess and compare the financial positions of North Carolina county and municipal governments from fiscal year 2008 to 2014. We find support for isomorphism as the dispersion of several indicators declined in the post-implementation period without offsetting beneficial changes in the mean indicator value. These findings pose a dilemma for the quantitative evaluation of both benchmarking and performance management systems; could offsetting changes result in null findings at the mean of the distribution?

t: Where Do Policy Innovations Come From?
abs: Organizations continuously need to balance competing needs for stability and change. Stability is required to routinize processes and achieve higher levels of efficiency. Change is needed to adapt to environmental changes and new demands. March (1991) coined this as a balance between organizational “exploitation” and “exploration.” Research in general management and strategy has explored this topic and how organizations, in different ways and with different results, seek to balance opposing needs for exploiting already developed capabilities with exploration efforts targeting innovation and change. Relatively little research has considered this topic in the public sector. Instead, the public sector has traditionally been associated with organizational stability. The Weberian bureaucracy values organizational efficiency and impartiality by disassociating positions and the people who occupy them. Bureaucrats are not expected to innovate or move “outside the box” but to work according to rules and procedures that ensures stability in problem solving and service delivery. Yet, organizations in the public sector also work in a dynamic world where demands and expectations are evolving, and change and adaptability are often not options but requirements. How public sector organizations address the exploration challenge still remains relatively understudied, and we know remarkably little about why some public organizations seem to embrace innovation much more than others. In his book Bureaucratic Ambition: Careers, Motives, and the Innovative Administrator, Teodoro sets out to investigate this question. Teodoro takes a mostly individual perspective and explores the role of top managers in shaping stability and change in organizations. This perspective is aligned with upper-echelon theory and the idea that organizations are reflections of their top management (Hambrick and Mason 1984). The main argument is that public managers (mid-level bureaucrats) come with different motives and work in different incentive structures which together spark their likelihood of entrepreneurial action. As Teodoro also recognizes, focusing on individual executives as policy entrepreneurs is not a new idea. For instance, in his fundamental treatise on bureaucracy, Wilson (1989) notes that remarkable policy entrepreneurs drive change. The main contribution of Teodoro’s book is that it outlines a theory of policy innovations to explain why some organizations embrace innovations while others hardly ever change. While we have seen studies predicting elements of change in public organizations, few scholars have sought to present a coherent theory taking into account both individual motives and contextual factors. As such, Bureaucratic Ambition is a welcome contribution to our understanding of public organizations. Scholars have for decades been interested in understanding organizational change and development over time. Many different approaches, theoretically and methodologically, have been employed in this endeavor. Some studies have focused on the role of individuals (or groups of individuals) and their objectives, values, and power while others focus on organizations and their needs and requirements. Already in the title, Bureaucratic Ambition positions itself somewhere in the middle of this debate. That organizations are important is signified with the word “bureaucratic” which relates to a distinct organizational form element. “Ambition” on the other hand is more agentic and focused on the individual who may (or may not) be ambitious. This duality between the bureaucracy that in its very nature is stable and durable, and ambition that is individual, change-oriented, and challenging status quo is what makes innovation in public organizations extremely complex. When are the bureaucratic forces strong enough to maintain status quo? When are ambitious individuals persistent and savvy enough to implement innovation and change? Or, put in March’s words, how is the balance point between exploitation and exploration decided over time (March 1991)? In Bureaucratic Ambition, Teodoro proposes that ambitious managers drive policy innovation. Ambition is a function of the opportunity structure in which a manager exists and the motives that he or she carries to the job. More elegantly phrased in the book, “ambition occurs when the motivational rubber meets the opportunity road” (p. 72). These two main building blocks, opportunity and motives, also reflects the multilevel dynamic that shapes change. Intrapersonal motives work together with an externally generated, interorganizational opportunity structure. The opportunity structure, which, according to Teodoro, is important in shaping ambition, is the incentives provided by the labor market. Some bureaucrats work in organizations where new managers are promoted from within. Such a vertical labor market values consistency and the ability of employees and managers to follow organizational expectations. This type of organization, in March’s typology focuses on exploiting existing capabilities to ensure stability, predictability, and efficiency in its operations. Other organizations tend to hire new managers from outside. Bureaucrats existing in a labor market where diagonal careers, or ramps, are the norm face a completely different incentive structure. Here, policy innovation is rewarded in the market, and organizations are likely to hire new managers that have proved themselves effective in implementing organizational changes. The balance consequently tips, and bureaucrats in these labor markets explore new opportunities rather than exploiting old certainties. Teodoro proposes that bureaucrats in diagonal labor markets pursue policy innovations because it demonstrates competence and positions them for future career moves. Bureaucrats in vertical labor markets are agents in traditional principal-agent relationships who are rewarded for behavior that complies with norms and expectations. Teodoro argues further that labor market differences are only half the explanation of policy innovation. Where opportunity structures predict the direction a bureaucrat takes an organization, individual motives (or needs) explain the strength of the force with which he or she does so. To make this argument, Teodoro draws on research in psychology. More specifically, it is proposed that bureaucrats with high needs for power and high needs for achievement are more likely to strongly pursue policies activities. Those with strong achievement motives are more likely to prosper in diagonal labor markets where innovations are rewarded, whereas those with strong power motives are more likely to succeed in vertical structures where power and influence are gained with internal promotions. Bureaucratic Ambition is a well-structured book. To me, chapter 3 is the most compelling chapter in the book where the theory of bureaucratic ambition is outlined in detail. The theory is original, at places thought-provoking, and firmly grounded in existing knowledge. By paying due respect to the work that he builds on, Teodoro is able to make his own contribution clear. A good theory should provide some degree of order in the complex social world. Teodoro’s theory does just that. Drawing on explicit assumptions about rationality as well as disparate strands of literature, Bureaucratic Ambition offers a compelling and plausible explanation for why some bureaucrats pursue change and others not. The theory chapter ends with a number of empirically testable hypotheses that aids in bridging the abstract theoretical world with empirical realities. Theories need to provide order in chaos. In doing so they have to focus more on some things than others. This is also the case here. Teodoro’s theory outlines why and how bureaucrats may pursue innovations. However, in taking this focus he also plays down the role that organizations play in shaping their own development. For instance, Greenwood and Hinings (1993), in their study of change in English local governments, find that local government organizations tend to conform to organizational patterns or “archetypes.” That is, organizations of a certain type are likely to pursue changes that are congruent with their distinct archetype. Other types of organizations conform to different archetypes, and are consequently likely to pursue different types of change efforts. This theory thoroughly downplays the roles that actors, bureaucrats, play in designing and promoting change and highlights how field-level institutional forces are important. Where Greenwood and Hinings (and other studies in the sociological institutional tradition) may be criticized for being too structural, Bureaucratic Ambition, on the other hand, may be too agentic in its focus. There is little room in the theory for organizational differences in their needs for change, for instance, caused by history or idiosyncratic challenges. It would be interesting to see what happens when bureaucratic ambition meets different types of organizational requirements. We see some hints of these types of dynamics in the case studies presented in chapter 2, but they are less visible in the theorizing and the quantitative studies. Bureaucratic Ambition is not a theoretical disposition. Besides its theoretical grounding, the book also presents some fascinating empirical studies. Teodoro should be commended for combining illustrative case studies with more classical deductive analysis in the later chapters. The cases in chapter 2 provide examples of bureaucratic ambition “in action.” The cases are easy to follow and provide the reader with a good understanding of not only the main topic of the book but also of the contexts of water utilities and police departments in the United States. As a non-American reader, I found these cases very useful; enough detail was provided to allow me to compare and contrast with local contexts that I am more familiar with. In chapters 4 through 6, a series of three empirical studies tests the hypotheses presented in chapter 3. While the results lend support to the theory, I find the studies equally useful in showing how the theory can be operationalized. This is an important step to link to future studies in this area of research. The empirical studies draw on relevant data, and Teodoro does a nice job in carefully interpreting results. While results are consistent with the theory, I do think studies that are more robust are needed to further substantiate the findings. For instance, in chapter 4 it is tested whether policy innovations are more likely when managers follow diagonal career paths (as predicted in the theory), yet the study cannot forcefully rule out reverse causality and that when organizations are in need of innovations they hire managers from the outside. The difference may appear subtle but the theoretical mechanism driving change would be different. Organizational innovation and change is one of the most elusive topics in organizational research. Organizations constantly balance opposing needs for exploiting what they are good at with exploring new ways of doing things that correspond with changing environments. Bureaucratic Ambition provides a compelling theory that provides an explanation for why and how organizations accomplish this balancing act in different ways. After the book is closed, the reader does not sit with a feeling that everything about organizational stability and change is now explained. Indeed, no single book would be able to provide such a feeling. I finished the book with a feeling of being more enlightened but also with a lot of questions and inspiration about where research might go next. As mentioned, the book recognizes that individuals and organizations together shape the need and implementation of policy innovations. To some degree, this is also reflected in the empirical analyses, for instance when organization size and location is brought into the picture. Still, I miss a greater attention to organizational differences, and how organizations to different extents may be in need of (or desire) innovation. What happens if an ambitious bureaucrat ends up in a place with little need for change? Will she pursue change anyways? Will such unnecessary change be less valued in the future labor market? It might also be interesting to take a closer look at the policy innovations that are implemented (or not implemented) and their consequences. Teodoro does recognize that adopting innovations in professional organizations is often as much about conforming to expectations as it is about improving effectiveness. Institutional theory would tell us that ceremonial changes might not yield great results. Does that affect subsequent career outcomes? Finally, while developed and tested in an American setting, the theory that is proposed is not country-specific. It is developed based on basic human motives and variation in career structures that can be found around the world. I think it would be interesting to see comparative work in this field. This could illuminate how different cultures or political systems work similarly and differently. The mechanisms underlying organizational change and innovation are important to understand, as they are the basis for future organizational development. Especially in developing countries where public administration is still maturing, understanding forces of change and stability is important. Bureaucratic ambition may not be the only explanation but seems like a plausible part of the puzzle. Bureaucratic Ambition is a timely book that contributes to our knowledge in important ways. It is very accessible and should be read by audiences interested in increasing their understanding of organizational life in government agencies. Further, it is a great example of how knowledge of public administration can be advanced by drawing on different methods and, not least, different disciplinary literatures. Research from public administration, political science, and psychology is combined to provide a theoretical account that provides useful insights, actionable knowledge, and inspiration for future research.

t: Adopt or Adapt? Unpacking the Role of Institutional Work Processes in the Implementation of New Regulations
abs: Building on a longitudinal study of the implementation of a new regulation and a framework of institutional work, this article makes three contributions: first, it explains how nonpowerful regulatees, by engaging in mobilization and cultivation, can change the power balance in the field and adjust the regulation to their local setting. Second, it takes a processual view and develops a conceptual model of how the implementation process unfolds through four waves; initial impact, response, recovery, and stabilization. Third, it shows how the studied actors combine contradictory institutional logics to legitimize their practices and resolve institutional complexity. Thus, it adds new insights into how actors, by engaging in collective and discursive institutional work, can influence both the implementation process and the regulation itself.

t: Partisan Advisers as Policy Workers: The Exceptionalism Put in Perspective
abs: Traditionally, partisan advisers to executive politicians have been studied from the vantage point of the politics-administration dichotomy, where their existence and role is more or less problematized (depending on the author’s normative standpoint) given that they do not fit neatly in the dichotomous view of political-administrative systems, and given the atypical accountability regimes under which they fall (Peters and Pierre 2004). Empirical developments in the last decade and a half—the growth in the number of partisan advisers, the broadening of their range of duties in many countries in the West, and a number of scandals involving ministerial advisers in various political-administrative systems—have helped to direct more scholarly attention to advisers. Deeper analytical questions concerning advisers have been pushed to the fore that go beyond the statutory issues and biographical profiles of earlier studies. These new types of questions are more concerned with what type of day-to-day activities ministerial advisers actually fulfill, what their added value is in the process of governance, and what their de facto place is in relation to ministers and the standing bureaucracy on the internal sphere as well as towards parliament, the media, and interest groups in the external sphere (Hustedt et al. 2017; Shaw and Eichbaum 2015). Craft’s 2016 book Backrooms and Beyond, which aims to offer a better understanding of how partisan advisers in Canada contribute to policy work itself, deserves a prominent place in this recent wave of enquiry into ministerial advisers. In part motivated by his own experience as a civil servant in the Canadian federal public service and later as a legislative assistant for a member of a Provincial Parliament, Craft delves into the backrooms of government to examine how political staffs engage in policymaking and consider implications of that activity for contemporary executive governance. The starting point of the book is the enduring debate between two opposing views on what political staffs should do, which, for Canada, can be traced back to the late 1960s. J. R. Mallory, who was one of the first scholars to research Canadian exempt staffs, found it, “clearly undesirable that a considerable number of persons not part of the civil service should be interposed between a Minister and his department” (p.6). Not much later, however, Paul Tellier, a top-ranking civil servant, would argue that partisan advisers did exactly what Mallory condemned, but that ministers should make better use of them. In sharp contrast to Mallory, Tellier regarded political staff as one corner of a new praiseworthy trilateral political-administrative arrangement (p.7). The debate continues to the present day with critical views under the heading of New Political Governance (Aucoin 2012) and more relaxed assessments of partisan elements in executive governance as Craft’s book represents. Salient scandals like the Canadian “sponsorship” scandal have given rise to questions regarding the appropriate accountability regimes for political staffs, but these are not the main focus of Craft’s inquiry. Instead, he argues that political staffs, and in particular partisan advisers, also deserve attention as policy workers. They have matured into actors whose daily practices are consequential to policymaking and therefore should be researched with a wider focus than just their accountability. The main question Crafts wants to provide an answer to is: how influential are partisan advisers as policy workers? Craft sets out to provide an exploratory comparative examination of advisers’ policy work and how this work intersects with others within the core executive at various points in the policy process. The three cases selected for comparison are the Canadian federal level and the provincial levels in British Columbia and New Brunswick. In addition to practical considerations, the cases were selected based on variation in centralization and institutional size and complexity, where the federal level naturally is the largest and most complex, British Columbia is a middle-scoring case, and New Brunswick represents a small government with an “intimate political administrative space” (p. 41). In each of the cases, both first ministers’ and ministers’ partisan advisers are examined. In chapter 1, the author develops his analytical framework. Craft articulates two binary scales: the type of policy activity (substantive or procedural) and the nature of policy interactions (advisory or non-advisory). Combining both dimensions leads to four types of policy work: buffering, bridging, moving, and shaping. Buffering refers to substantive policy advisory activities whereas bridging refers to procedural policy advisory activities. Shaping refers to content-based non-advisory policy work, and moving refers top process-based non-advisory policy work. This framework anchors the rest of the book and structures the empirical chapters. Chapter two brings the reader up to date on Canadian partisan advisers in the tradition of the first wave of research on ministerial advisers, providing basic descriptive details on the size of Cabinet, public service, and partisan advisers as well as the relevant governance arrangements in each case. An insightful historical overview of the evolution of partisan advisers in Canada is also given, showing a pattern of institutionalization, expansion, and specialization across the three cases. The next four chapters present a very rich addition to the mentioned second wave of research on advisers by examining advisers’ contemporary policy work, structured along Craft’s four-fold conceptualization of policy work. Craft spoke with assistants of deputy ministers, senior cabinet office officials, deputy ministers, ministers, partisan advisers in Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), ministerial partisan advisers, directors of minister’s office, and many former officials. Based on the assumption that partisan advisers have up until now been understood to be mere political operatives, the core argument of the book is that if we take a closer look at partisan advisers’ policy practices, what we actually see is policy workers—in the sense of actors who contribute to policymaking and its outcomes—albeit with partisan links. Partisan advisers have become established systematic features of the core executive. This argument is vividly developed and convincingly demonstrated throughout the book. It effectively brings the study of ministerial advisers more in tune with the broader study of policy work, and particularly policy advisory systems. On a critical note, the author at points seems to overstate the dominance of the initial notion that partisan advisers have thus far been regarded as mere political operatives, for the sake of making his core argument. In addition, although the study investigates four departments per case, the departments are not specified (other than the PMO and the respective First Minister’s Offices) to ensure participants anonymity. Although this choice is understandable, it is also regrettable because more emphasis on policy-sectoral differences would have added to the study’s value. The book is thoroughly successful in achieving its overall goal to offer improved conceptual and empirical accounts of policy work through an analysis of Canadian partisan advisers. Conceptually, the book makes important steps in bridging the gap between studies of political-administrative relations and policy studies. The conceptualization of advisers in terms of buffers, bridges, shapers, and movers is valuable and deserves to be applied more broadly in other political-administrative systems. It holds promise for insightful future cross-national comparisons and can complement other conceptualizations (for instance those developed by Connaugthon 2010 and Maley 2000). However, the largest contribution of Backrooms and Beyond is empirical. Its detailed account reminds us that nonpartisan policy work is not monopolized by the career civil service; partisan advisers’ broad role in the policy process should be regarded with systematic and thorough attention by anyone who wishes to understand the workings of the core executive. By looking past the customary normative questions about accountability and the crowding-out of nonpartisan input, the book helps the “normalization” of partisan advisers in the sense that they are all-around policy workers who enrich the policy process with their distinct rationale. As Craft states, “Ultimately, policy-making is a political activity” (p. 251).

t: Agency Performance Challenges and Agency Politicization
abs: In this article we evaluate the relationship between political control and bureaucratic performance using information requested by researchers via Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests and Congress via congressional committee requests. The information requested was the same, and the timing of requests was similar. We find modest evidence of a relationship between agency politicization and a lack of responsiveness to requests for information from the public and Congress. Politicized agencies are slower to respond to requests even when controlling for agency size and workload. There is little evidence, however, that these agencies are more likely to respond poorly when they do respond. The difficulties in responding appear to be due to poor performance of the FOIA offices, either because political actors focus more on other agency activities or because of poorer management agency-wide. We conclude that efforts to make agencies responsive to elected officials may hurt management performance.

t: Dual Dynamics: A New Theory of the Relationship Between Congress and the Bureaucracy
abs: This book offers a new and important perspective on the relationship between Congress and the bureaucracy. Its most significant contribution is to argue and show how the bureaucracy performs three crucial functions in government: bureaucracies monitor problems, they help to define the problems they monitor for action at higher levels of government, and they generate and transmit information about problems to policy makers in Congress. Few would probably disagree with this characterization of the bureaucracy, but Workman convincingly argues that these functions of the bureaucracy have been given too little scholarly attention in previous treatments of the role of bureaucracy. According to Workman, much research has placed too much emphasis on how the bureaucracy can be controlled and on how the bureaucracy can influence the backend of the policy making process, including the implementation of policies and regulation. Workman’s main concern is the role of the bureaucracy in the front end of the policy making process; how it influences and shapes the Congressional agenda by providing signals and information about problems in need of political action. The bureaucracy, however, also receives cues and signals from Congress, and this tension between democratic authority and bureaucratic expertise forms what Workman denotes the dual dynamics of agenda setting. In short, the dual dynamics implies that change in the policy agenda is a result of bureaucratic problem solving from below and congressional problem prioritization from above. Thus, a central task for bureaucracies is to monitor problems and aid in defining them for government actions, whereas Congress then synthesizes this vast information, handles tradeoffs among which issues to attend to, and coordinates action on the policy problems. In chapter 2, Workman lays out how his perspective on the relations between Congress and the bureaucracy deviates not only from standard views on the bureaucracy but also from how the policy making process is normally understood. This critical literature review is highly recommendable and deserves to be on the curriculum of every graduate course on public administration. Every scholar must carve out a niche for his or her own study, but Workman does not place his study in a remote niche of the field of public administration. Instead, he places himself right in the centerfield where politics and administration intersects. From that vantage point he engages in a critical discussion with, for instance, the delegation literature, agency theory, and research on subsystem politics—literatures that, according to Workman, are at risk of getting lost in the details and of losing sight of the big and important questions of the discipline. As Workman describes: “It is very much like holding an object in one’s line of sight and drawing the object ever closer. In doing so, details of the object come into focus, while the object, its general nature and contours are lost. This has been the course of scholarship on the bureaucracy until very recently” (p. 25). Another critique is directed at the strong scholarly emphasis on accountability and democratic responsiveness. If this can be achieved along with solving the policy problems at hand, all is well and good. But sometimes, as Workman argues, responsiveness and accountability comes at the expense of addressing severe policy problems, and this tension between responsive government and problem-solving government provides another central motivation for the book (p. 46). Furthermore, Workman concludes his comprehensive literature review with a sharp comment to modern trends in the disciplines of public policy and public administration: Today’s scholars both in the United States and elsewhere prefer to study and discuss the virtues of voluntary regulation, networks, clubs, market mechanisms, and other forms of ‘governance’ or ‘steering’. Yet, the presumed demise of traditional forms of bureaucracy belies the centrality and visibility of bureaucrats in policy making and their ability to influence how government addresses problems. Today’s forms of governing are much like yesterday’s forms of governing. (p. 61) Though the dual dynamics argument is plausible and relatively straightforward, it involves some challenging concepts and demanding expectations. Information, problem space, solution space, issue shuffling, and issue bundling, for instance, are concepts that are not easily defined and very difficult to operationalize. Furthermore, the dual dynamics argument implies a reciprocal relationship between Congress and the bureaucracy, and such two-way causality is notoriously difficult to investigate empirically. Thus, as the theoretical argument of the book evolves, one may begin to wonder if Workman really can provide empirical evidence on the theorized mechanisms. The answer is both yes and no. The empirical foundation of Workman’s analysis of dual dynamics is an examination of the agendas of the bureaucracy and Congress over the past quarter-century. As an indicator of the signals from the bureaucracy, he collects and codes more than 200,000 federal regulations. By content coding these regulations based on the same issue coding approach used in the Policy Agendas Project, he is able to compare this bureaucratic agenda with a measure of the Congressional agenda based on a similar coding of congressional hearings. The issue coding, as argued by Workman, provides substance to these data and gets him closer to the dynamics of the policy making process. In addition, the large scale data approach allows Workman to assess general, system-level characteristics of the US policy making process instead of narrowing in on just one agency or one policy domain. When it comes to the thorny question of how to study information quality and signals from the bureaucracy, Workman finds inspiration in communications research. Particularly, he develops measures of the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and signal amplitudes, both of which are based on particular patterns of change and stability in the issue agendas. In addition, he creatively applies a variety of other relevant measures and methodological tools such as entropi scores and biplots; the latter to get closer at the issue bundling dynamics (e.g., p. 121). The empirical analysis of this book is truly creative, and the scope of the data is impressive. In that way, Workman comes a long way in providing empirical evidence in support of the model of dual dynamics. He also comes much further in identifying these dynamics than anyone before him. Yet, there are still some nagging questions left for empirical and theoretical scrutiny in future studies. Many of these would require massive additional data collection and coding, but, given the scope of the theoretical claims, this may be a necessary investment. One approach which might be feasible would be to investigate the link between the different agendas at a more disaggregated level. Issue interdependences justify the use of more complex measures such as entropy and SNR ratios, but still it would be relevant to investigate more direct, issue-to-issue correlations between federal regulations and congressional hearings. Another, more challenging question is how much of the bureaucratic agenda regards problem monitoring and problem definition, and how much is about solutions and implementation. In other words, Workman describes the nature and contours of the dual dynamics phenomenon; the next step is to bore deeper into the details of the subject and the causal linkages of the phenomenon. An avenue that may be further developed in this theoretical framework is the influence of Congress on the bureaucracy. In chapter 5, when Workman analyses how Congress influences the signaling of policy problems by the federal bureaucracy, the main driver of political influence is partisan control of Congress. This is justified with a brief reference to issue-ownership theory, which claims that the parties have different issue priorities. This is definitely one plausible source of issue priorities in Congress, but given the problem-oriented focus of the book, it is a little surprising that this election-generated shift in the party control of Congress should be the main source of political influence on bureaucratic signals and priorities. The book is about US politics, but the theoretical argument regards questions and challenges of relevance to all democratic, political systems. Therefore, it is worth reflecting on the extent the argument and empirical results may generalize outside the US system. Central to Workman’s argument is the assumption of a very pluralistic system, where information is in over supply and where competing bureaucracies have strong incentives to provide the information that the politicians demand. For instance, Workman’s analysis of how many agencies issue regulation within a given issue domain is striking (p. 124). This pattern is probably very different in smaller parliamentary systems characterized by centralized and hierarchically structured bureaucracies working within clearly defined issue jurisdictions. Furthermore, in most parliamentary systems the executive government de facto monopolizes the bureaucracy, which means that the legislators often do not have their own bureaucracy. Dual dynamics must still be at play, but the exact mechanisms may look very different than the one revealed by Workman. Workman’s book offers an innovative and important new research agenda. It is a research agenda with much potential, including pulling public administration back into the center of political science. It is also an ambitious research agenda that may require fundamentally new empirical approaches in order to fulfill its promises. It will be interesting to see how the field of public administration responds to Workman’s invitation: with ignorance or excitement?

t: Balancing Relations and Results in Regional Networks of Public-Policy Implementation
abs: Regional networks have become popular routes for central governments to translate national ambitions into regional policies and actions; but these networks face challenges, having to balance between the dual objectives of obtaining short-term goals and establishing enduring network relations. This empirical article addresses the question as to whether there is any tension between these objectives, and if so, how can it be explained and managed. We report two studies on regional networks in the public-policy areas of Education and Employment in the Netherlands. Multiple methods were used: Interviews, surveys, archival records, social network data, and participatory observations. The findings suggest that this tension exists, and that it is especially found in young networks; more mature networks demonstrate better balance between network relations and goal attainment. Network governance was found to be a key explanatory factor whereby a network which had an administrative organization with a merely facilitative role, performed best in both respects.

t: Compensating for Poor Performance with Promotional Symbols: Evidence from a Survey Experiment
abs: Extant literature regarding citizens’ responses to government public communications focuses on the roles of transparency and provision of information. Conversely, the effect of strategically designed symbols, which are integral to most public communications, received limited attention. Building on social psychology and marketing research, we theorize that familiar promotional symbols enhance citizens’ positive attitudes toward government through “evaluative conditioning,” yet this effect is conditioned by citizens’ experiences of actual government performance. We test these expectations via a survey experiment, which examines participants’ responses to a familiar promotional symbol of an Israeli state-owned electricity monopoly, given near-random variation in their experiences of prolonged power outages. We find that exposure to the well-known symbol enhances participants’ favorable attitudes toward the organization, and that this effect extends to those who recently experienced poor electricity services. The effect is significant in relation to participants’ trust in the organization, but not regarding their satisfaction and performance evaluation. These findings indicate that familiar promotional symbols can shape citizens’ attitudes, and compensate for the effect of poor performance, with regard to sufficiently ambiguous organizational aspects. We discuss the implications of these findings for current research on the effectiveness of transparency and performance information.

t: Black in Blue: Racial Profiling and Representative Bureaucracy in Policing Revisited
abs: This study examines the association between the degree to which a police force is ethnically representative of the population it serves and the force’s engagement in racial profiling as a policing tactic. Evidence for this study comes from English and Welsh police forces that implemented force-specific recruitment targets for officers from ethnic minority backgrounds between 2000 and 2010. Results suggest that an increase in the proportion of ethnic minorities on a police force is significantly associated with a decrease in the proportion of ethnic minorities that are stopped and searched by that police force. We also examine whether the effects of representative bureaucracy accrue nonlinearly or dynamically. This analysis failed to produce strong evidence for the “reform fatigue” and “diversity fatigue” hypotheses. Finally, we demonstrate that active representation has primarily occurred in forces in which racial profiling was intensively used as a policing tactic. These findings have implications for the democratic legitimacy of representative bureaucracy.

t: Review of Transparency and the Open Society: Practical Lessons for Effective Policy
abs: Transparency and the Open Society: Practical Lessons for Effective Policy by Roger Taylor and Tim Kelsey builds upon and pushes the transparency literature forward. The authors rely heavily on medical examples with an emphasis on the UK’s National Health Service to build and highlight their arguments. This book should be recommended reading for students of governmental transparency because of its focus away from government-driven transparency to relying on private entities as necessary partners to achieve transparency and assess the fairness of policy outcomes for individuals and populations. While the public management literature has been moving toward a theory of open government (Meijer et al. 2012; Piotrowski 2016), and many of the examples and models Taylor and Kelsey discuss fall within these broader definitions, the authors frame their work within the more narrow transparency literature. Both Taylor and Kelsey have years of experience as practitioners in the open data field. Roger Taylor co-founded the Open Public Services Network at the Royal Society of Arts in London. The Open Public Services Network is a program that provides an independent assessment of government and public services performance data. Tim Kelsey served as the British government’s first director of transparency and open data. Together Taylor and Kelsey co-founded Dr Foster, a company that collects and publishes healthcare information. The perspective the two bring is a pragmatic one that helps inform the academic discussion in this field. The authors have two primary propositions, which they elaborate on within the book: “That transparency does not increase with the volume of information provided to the individuals. It increases only to the degree I have information that can evidence whether I am being treated fairly;” and “That transparency, by this definition, requires shared access to underlying raw granular data” (p. 2). Their model is sound when considering transparency outcomes of public programs but does not address transparency of process or programs which do not directly involve individuals. They begin with a history of transparency and related concepts and set out a rationale for their propositions. The authors identify three historical traditions of transparency: politics, economics, and science. They argue that the access to information (ati) or freedom of information (foi) movement is born out of the politics tradition. They see disclosure, primarily forced disclosure, as an outgrowth of the economics tradition. Lastly, they argue that the data sharing movement comes out of the science tradition. Their synthesis and analysis of the origins of transparency is clear and well presented. Their summary table of the method, description, structure, and aim of the three approaches to transparency (p. 28) will definitely be well cited and replicated in future work. In the end, this may be their main contribution to the literature. They also present a summary of well-known costs and unintended harms, which are attributed to transparency. Taylor and Kelsey argue that “data sharing is the foundational mechanism for transparency” (p. 53) and are clearly building upon their applied experiences to make this argument. Throughout the book, a series of very good mini-case studies illustrate the points the authors are making. They state that their contribution is a logic model: (1) the aim of transparency is fairness; (2) you need to see the outcomes of a system across populations to assess if it is fair; and (3) transparency driven by data sharing is going to require new instructional structures. The authors argue that transparency can act as an instrument of social justice and improvement. The later part of the book presents an analysis of a range of transparency initiatives, which are designed to combat corruption, inefficiency, and poor outcomes. They present the strengths and weaknesses of each initiative. They find two primary problems with respect to transparency based on data sharing: “how to adequately protect the privacy of individuals and the commercial secrets of companies in a world of data sharing” and “identifying the necessary institutional arrangements to ensure that access to data serves the public interest” (p. 4). They accurately capture two of the biggest issues around data sharing of outcome data with respect to public programs when dealing with individuals and populations. The chapter on “Surveillance, Transparency, and Privacy” is particularly relevant in today’s political context given the public’s increased understanding of the surveillance tools used by governments. Taylor and Kelsey argue that individuals need to be able to discern which organizations use data in ways that benefit the user (beneficial surveillance) and those that do not (harmful surveillance). It is important to note that the book is not solely focused on government organizations but also covers private entities such as hospitals and retailers (e.g., Amazon). Oversight of national security surveillance programs is more difficult than overseeing a hospital, but Taylor and Kelsey believe it is not impossible. They state, “Oversight of security arrangements would be greatly enhanced if those responsible had access to the data and the technical capacity to genuinely interrogate and test the narrative offered by those they oversee; to be able to form their own judgement as to the efficacy of security agencies” (p. 302). They proceed with a discussion of allowing individuals to opt-in or opt-out of monitoring and surveillance. This an avenue researchers could pursue empirically. Their discussion is an excellent contribution to the debate and extremely time given the recent revelations. The authors do a thorough job of building their argument, but the reader is left with the question “Who then do we trust to analyze government data?” Taylor and Kelsey focus on nongovernmental organizations being involved in the dissemination of government information. They believe that you need to pry the data out of the hands of government and let outside entities analyze it to have an adequate review of outcomes. They discuss the roles of civil society organizations, corporations, and universities in this oversight process. While they propose different relationships, they do not give an explicit roadmap. They state “[i]t would be foolhardy to try to predict exactly how the organisational infrastructure of data sharing will develop in future decades” (p. 277). A reader is still left trying to imagine what these new institutional models would look like and understand if they are the most appropriate ones. If private organizations are going to be the ones who primarily analyze government programs, what oversight tools will be available to hold the private entities to account? These new relationships in transparency oversight serve as possible cases to study for scholars of networks and collaborative governance (Emerson et al. 2012). Another significant contribution of the book is the focus on both individual level and population level data. This focus on fairness at the population level is new and deserves serious consideration by scholars in the field. It should be highlighted that the authors focus on transparency of outcomes not on process. There is little discussion on transparency that is not related to the outcomes of large scale government programs. This is not a critique, since this is not the authors’ focus, but is highlighted to show how their work differs from others in the field. Overall Taylor and Kelsey present an interesting shift in the way we consider transparency and the roles nongovernmental entities could play in assuring fairness of public services.

t: Enhancing Public Innovation by Transforming Public Governance, or vice versa?
abs: The book Enhancing Public Innovation by Transforming Public Governance, edited by Jacob Torfing and Peter Triantafillou, departs from the view that public innovation is needed to address societal challenges in times of changing expectations and interactions between citizens and the state, as well as fiscal constraints. Similar to other books on innovation in the public sector (e.g., Bekkers, Edelenbos, and Steijn 2011), it rejects the view that the public sector is incapable of innovation. Instead, the book aims to contextualize innovation in the public sector by paying explicit attention to the institutions of governance that surround processes of innovation. Three ideal type governance paradigms—classical public administration, new public management, and new public governance—are argued to both facilitate and impede innovation in distinct ways. The central thesis of the book is that institutions of governance must be transformed in order to spur innovation in the public sector: “The overarching idea of this edited volume is that the way we shape the institutional forms of governance in the public sector affects its capacity for innovation” (p. 3). More specifically, the editors of the book argue that governance must be tailored more toward the paradigm of new public governance without losing sight of the aspects of classical public administration and new public management that may be conducive for public innovation. For the editors, new public governance—“the new kid on the block”—with its focus on collaboration, integrative leadership, and trust-based management, holds the most promise to facilitate public innovations that are needed to address today’s societal problems.

t: Winners and Losers in the Ecology of Games: Network Position, Connectivity, and the Benefits of Collaborative Governance Regimes
abs: Collaborative governance regimes (CGRs) are often viewed as a means to be more inclusive of diverse actors than other forms of governance. However, collaboration can also reinforce pre-existing power and resource dynamics instead of distributing resources and facilitating joint action. This article tests seven hypotheses concerning how the structural position of an actor within a policy network influences said actor’s ability to access resources through participation in CGRs. We then test these hypotheses using data generated by a survey of 400 actors within a regional environmental governance network that contains 57 CGRs. Using exponential random graph models (ERGMs) designed to account for network dependencies, we test how various attributes of network structure—in terms of an actor’s connections to other actors and to CGRs—influence that actor’s ability to access resources through CGR participation. We find that actors who benefit from participation in one CGR are more likely to benefit from participation in other CGRs as well, speaking to the potential for CGRs to further existing imbalances rather than distribute benefits more equitably. Further, CGRs that foster principled engagement (increased face-to-face communication, development of common problem understanding, and awareness of other network actors) are strongly associated with actors’ ability to access financial, human, and technical resources through participation. Although the CGRs we study do improve actors’ access to network resources, this can occur in ways that further existing inequities in resource access.

t: Gleaning Insights from a Seasoned Practitioner’s Playbook
abs: Ira Goldstein wrote the The Federal Management Playbook for practitioners working in, or engaging with, federal agencies. For this purpose, the book holds true to its title, providing a well organized, well written, and straightforward guide for navigating the increasingly complex and uncertain federal landscape. Goldstein draws on his extensive managerial experience, interviews, case studies, and academic literature to outline workable strategies for succeeding as a manager working in or with the federal government. Although Goldstein wrote The Federal Management Playbook for practitioners, the book has much to offer public management scholars. The book is a rare opportunity for a glimpse inside the mind of a public servant whose nearly half-century experience ranges from working for a defense contractor during the Vietnam War to serving as Comptroller General at the Government Accountability Office to playing a leading role in creating Deloitte’s federal consulting business. Goldstein’s tenure and the weight of his experience demands public management scholars pay attention. We are well beyond the period when public administration scholars played central practitioner roles and we have seen scholars raise alarms and offer suggestions for bridging the divide between scholarship and practice (e.g., Moynihan 2015; Raadschelders and Lee 2011). Bridging the gap requires us to engage practitioners on several fronts, including reading their insights on management and administration. Books like Goldstein’s can inform our research by giving us perspective on the challenges and opportunities public managers believe are the most critical to their craft. In this review, I provide a basic overview of Goldstein’s book, highlighting sections and themes that may be of particular interest to public management scholars. Goldstein outlines a basic framework consisting of four knowledge-based dimensions of success that define what managers should focus on and three strategic phases of action that describe how managers should organize and execute those dimensions. The four dimensions of success are goal definition, stakeholder impact, resources, and timeframes. First, Goldstein argues, choosing and communicating achievable goals is a critical management activity with important implications for program success. Second, program success also requires that managers understand and frequently engage key interest groups and stakeholders. Third, managers must expertly define and deploy the resources necessary––people, processes, and technology––for getting the job done. Finally, managers must establish strategic timeframes throughout implementation so that program milestones sync with political, organizational, and resource needs. Successful managers engage the four dimensions through a series of three strategic phases––planning, executing, and defending––as they implement federal programs and initiatives. Goldstein explores the implications of treating or ignoring the four dimensions and three strategic phases in a series of chapters dedicated to topics such as human relations, organizational design, technology, risk-taking, contracting, and innovation. The book closes with a series of chapters focused on issues relating to working with specific communities operating in the federal space: oversight organizations, civil servants, political appointees, and industry consultants. Goldstein applies his framework to issues that should be of particular interest to public management scholars, such as goal negotiation, the temporal elements of management, and workforce demographics. Enterprising researchers may find opportunities in Goldstein’s insights for rethinking or expanding existing theories and research in these areas. Public management and organization scholars have long understood the importance of goal setting (Locke and Latham 2002). Goals are critical for defining missions and securing employee motivation and stakeholder support. Goldstein discusses goal setting frequently in The Federal Management Playbook and much of what he says will not be surprising to those familiar with the goal setting literature. Researchers may glean new insights, however, from his discussion of goal negotiation as a critical skill for public managers. Goldstein argues that few understand the power and flexibility federal managers attain through goal negotiation. The outcomes of goal negotiations ultimately define the terms by which political principals, the public, and key stakeholders judge program success or failure. Negotiating achievable, coherent goals is becoming a critical management skill as the diversity of stakeholders participating in the provision of public goods and services increases essential and complex process. Distilling diverse goals and interests into concrete, achievable goals aligned with stakeholder interests, then, is a critical public management skill essential for organizational success. So far, public management scholars have not explored the dynamics and implications of goal negotiation. If it is critical to program success, as Goldstein suggests, researchers would do well to improve our understanding of the process and its implications for public outcomes. For example, do goal negotiations, holding program performance constant, increase the likelihood of program approval and survival? Does participating in goal negotiation increase stakeholder acceptance of programs and program performance? What determines whether goal negotiations are successful? Do network structures and dynamics have implications for the relative success or failure of goal negotiations? These are just a few of potentially many puzzles researchers might investigate. Goldstein’s treatment of the temporal factors of managing in the federal government should be of great interest to practitioners and scholars alike. For Goldstein, setting activities and goals according to near-term, midrange, and long-term timeframes is essential for achieving flexibility and establishing coherence between agency goals and the goals of the administration, its political appointees, and Congress. Setting short-term goals that build toward longer-term achievements affords managers better risk management and helps them achieve greater compatibility with actors and organizations operating according to timeframes dominated by the political cycle. Scholars may find Goldstein’s timeframe discussions a good starting point for further developing our understanding of goal setting’s temporal dimensions and their implications. Another topic Goldstein addresses that may be of interest to public management researchers is age diversity. Changing federal workforce demographics is a familiar, salient topic in the public management literature (Choi and Rainey 2014; Wilkins 2006). Although management scholars are increasingly paying attention to the implications of changing age demographics (Collins, Hair, and Rocco 2009), the issue has not received much attention from public management scholars. Goldstein draws on his own observations and research in psychology to argue that intentional generational integration may yield a powerful combination of knowledge and entrepreneurship. For example, although millennials have more education than previous generations, they lack Boomers’ experience and faith in bureaucracy. However, millennials are also less risk averse and less content to remain in static, predictable jobs. The millennial generation’s relative volatility may create significant challenges in a federal government that values stability and low turnover. Government agencies must challenge young talent to keep them motivated and to provide flexibility to compete with the private sector. Quickly moving young talent up the ranks may motivate younger workers while also promoting generational integration. Goldstein argues this practice not only yields positive results but also boosts continuity as the boomer generation retires. Changing age demographics may create opportunities for management to improve performance and increase innovation in the federal government, but it may also pose significant challenges. Placing younger managers in charge of older employees can disrupt established workplace age norms (Collins, Hair, and Rocco 2009). The higher average age of public sector workers, combined with the threat of a coming retirement tsunami in the federal government makes it critical that public management researchers improve our understanding of the implications of age diversity, or lack thereof, in government agencies and the efficacy of managing for age diversity. For many reasons, The Federal Management Playbook could not have had a timelier release. As I write this review, a new administration is taking the reins of the federal government, promising hiring freezes and other policy changes with big implications for how the federal government conducts business. Goldstein dedicates much of his focus to overcoming the challenges of operating as a permanent bureaucrat in the face of the uncertainty that accompanies the political cycle. However, he also considers the flip side of the transition, offering advice to political appointees dealing with permanent bureaucrats, such as grafting administration initiatives onto agency culture to increase the likelihood of their acceptance of the new administration’s agenda. Consulting Goldstein’s writings will be worthwhile as we observe federal agencies reacting and adapting to the new administration’s policies. Goldstein did not write this book for an academic audience, but when a practitioner with his tenure and experience puts their knowledge and expertise on paper it behooves us as public management scholars to read and understand this perspective. Although readers may find some aspects of the book repetitive (e.g., successful readers will have no trouble remembering the four dimensions and three phases of action) and simplistic, I believe The Federal Management Playbook deserves a spot on the bookshelves of public management scholars. I enjoyed this book and will recommend it to colleagues, practitioners, and students alike.

t: Management and Performance in US Nursing Homes
abs: Accountability pressures have generated complex performance measurement regimes to evaluate and improve public or publicly-funded services. Performance management, however, faces many challenges including the tradeoffs posed by numerous dimensions of performance and a lack of consensus on which organizational and environmental factors can improve these results. This study seeks to understand the effect of management and other factors on different dimensions and measures of performance in U.S. public, nonprofit, and for-profit nursing homes. Using a hybrid data set that combines archival government data on performance in nursing homes with a recent nursing home administrators’ survey, we find that innovative management significantly1 improves the quality of care. In addition, more innovation and less power sharing in management are associated with serving fewer Medicaid-funded clients. Significant differences in performance exist across public, nonprofit, and for-profit organizations. These differences are notable across both the archival and perceptual models of performance.

t: The Pathways That Make New Public Employees Committed: A Dual-Process Model Triggered by Newcomer Learning
abs: The current article proposes a dual-process model to explain how newcomer learning, an outcome of the early socialization experiences of new public employees, leads to organizational commitment in public organizations. Specifically, we argue that newcomer learning triggers two distinct psychological mechanisms: an affective pathway, leading to job satisfaction and ultimately to affective commitment, and a cognitive pathway, leading to psychological contract fulfillment and normative commitment. We conducted a two-wave survey with 728 newcomers in the Brazilian Internal Revenue Service to test this dual-pathway model. Our findings support the hypothesis that these affective and cognitive pathways constitute independent channels in mediating the impact of newcomer learning on public servants’ organizational commitment. Moreover, we observe that the affective component of commitment is triggered by job satisfaction, whereas the normative component is more closely linked with psychological contract fulfillment. Our findings highlight the importance of providing newcomers with the knowledge about organizational values, formal procedures and informal norms and skills to perform their roles during the early socialization period to strengthen their commitment to public organizations and ultimately to the public interest.

t: From Passive to Active Representation—Experimental Evidence on the Role of Normative Values in Shaping White and Minority Bureaucrats’ Policy Attitudes
abs: Studies of representative bureaucracy have shown how minority groups are often underrepresented in public agencies (passive representation) and that the match between bureaucrats’ and clients’ racial background has important impacts on minority groups (active representation). Much less attention has been devoted to the question of what influences this link from passive to active representation, and, in this case, what factors moderate how bureaucrats’ demographic background transforms into attitudes toward multicultural policies. A survey experiment among Texas school principals shows how emphasizing the normative value of ethnic and cultural differences increases the discrepancy between white and minority bureaucrats’ attitudes toward a minority-supportive policy. However, emphasizing that research-based evidence supports the policy makes all bureaucrats more positive. These results increase our understanding of how the link between passive and active representation can be moderated. Forschung zum Thema der repräsentativen Verwaltung hat gezeigt, dass Minderheiten in der öffentlichen Verwaltung oft unterrepräsentiert sind (passive Repräsentation) und dass Minderheiten profitieren, wenn Beamte und Bürger denselben (Migrations-)Hintergrund haben (aktive Repräsentation). Weniger bekannt ist dagegen, wann passive in aktive Repräsentation umschlägt und welche Faktoren diese Transformation beeinflussen. Ein Survey-Experiment mit Schuldirektoren in Texas zeigt, dass die Betonung des normativen Wertes ethnischer und kultureller Unterschiede den Kontrast zwischen der Denkweise von Direktoren, die der Mehrheit angehören und denen, die einer Minderheit angehören, in Bezug auf eine minderheitenfreundliche Politik verstärkt. Die Betonung von forschungsbasierenden Befunden zu Gunsten einer minderheitenfreundlichen Politik stimmt allerdings alle Direktoren positiver. Diese Ergebnisse verbessern unser Verständnis davon, inwieweit die Beziehung von passiver und aktiver Repräsentation moderiert wird. Note: Um die Übersetzungen der Zusammenfassungen übersichtlich und einfach verständlich zu gestalten, wurde bei allen personenbezogenen Bezeichnungen immer das generische Maskulinum verwendet, das sowohl Personen des männlichen als auch des weiblichen Geschlechts einschließt. Translation credit: Alexander Kroll of Florida International University and Johanna Smyth

t: Bureaucratic Race-Making and Place-Making Through the Lens of Policing
abs: Pulled Over takes an interdisciplinary approach in understanding the dynamics between race, policing, and citizenship. While combining literature from psychological, sociological, historical, legal, and criminological perspectives, Epp, Maynard-Moody, and Haider-Markel advance an argument that is undergirded by an organizational behavior perspective. They center on policing as an institution, arguing that racial disparities prosper due to institutional decisions and behavior. Specifically, the authors’ in-depth attention to a specific type of police activity—police stops—allows for a careful display of how systemic organizational processes produce racially disparate outcomes. In the current state of crisis with police-community relations around the United States, the national dialogue has been framed from various perspectives with some focusing on individual officers as “bad apples.” However, Pulled Over highlights the role that larger structural forces play in contributing to problems between police and the communities they serve. The authors utilize a mixed-method approach that includes a survey of over 2,300 drivers in the Kansas City Metropolitan Area as well as follow-up in-depth interviews with drivers, interviews with traffic officers, and focus groups with police officers. This study provides a unique contribution in considering perspective of drivers with in-depth incident details and police officer behavior rather than merely providing information from citation tickets like prior research. The results of quantitative and qualitative analyses confirm similar themes, which enriches the authors’ thesis about institutional factors contributing to racial disparities. The authors make two key arguments. First, they distinguish between two types of stops: traffic safety stops and investigatory stops. The main difference is an officer having a true justification for a stop versus a pretext. A true justification consists of an officer stopping a driver for the sole purpose of a traffic safety violation (which is often followed by a lecture on driving behavior). Alternatively, a pretext involves an officer using a minor violation that would not normally lead to a stop as a means to question a driver or search a vehicle. Examples of a pretext include failure to signal a lane change or a burned-out license plate light. While this distinction offers a typology by which to evaluate police traffic stops, the fine line separating the two stop types depicts how, even with red tape, official rules can be used to justify and accomplish one’s own ends. Second, the authors carefully describe a process by which bureaucrat behavior affects public perceptions and behaviors. They argue that formal policies and practices activate and reproduce negative cultural stereotypes which, in turn, influence police perceptions and subsequent police behaviors. This chain often results in investigatory stops targeted at blacks. These unfair investigatory stops, however, diminish blacks’ perceptions of the police, resulting in greater distrust of the police and a reconstructed meaning of the law, equal citizenship, and freedom as well as increased racial identity. This process moves beyond the traditional dialogue of individual racism and into the realm of examining bureaucratic actions and the impact of those actions on citizens. Herein, the authors emphasize how interactions between the bureaucrat and the citizen can shape the relationship between the citizen and the bureaucracy as a whole. For example, the authors note that black citizens who experience investigatory stops are less likely to participate in democratic processes such as voting, providing evidence of the spillover effects of investigatory stops. The authors’ argument encourages the reader to evaluate bureaucratic (police) behavior not only based on short-term benefits but also on long-term consequences. The text stresses the importance of looking at the dispersion of management techniques and front-line practices across geographic boundaries, bearing in mind the consequences of these practices. Moreover, the authors explain how the practice of investigatory stops are inconsistent with the stated goal of crime control. By detailing what we would have expected for this goal to be realized, the authors touch on the importance of measuring actual practice against intended goals. In advancing their claims, the authors not only provide thorough justification for their argument but also walk through alternative explanations to show why they are inadequate. Specifically, they show that blacks are stopped more because of implied stereotypes and associated biases that are inherent in the practice of investigatory stops. Likewise, the nature of investigatory stops alone calls for certain types of behavior by the officer (e.g., more intrusive behavior). They find that drivers are treated differently based on demographic characteristics, namely that young black men are subject to more intrusions during investigatory stops. To further support the propositions made in Pulled Over, the two main theoretical frameworks used are institutionalized racial framing and procedural justice. Institutionalized racial framing displays not only how race affects official government practices, but also how such practices further heighten negative stereotypes and racial divides. This theory is used to support the argument that investigatory stops further perpetuate racial divides and help define the social meaning of race. Second, from the onset of the book, the authors challenge some of the fundamental principles of procedural justice. One tenet of procedural justice rests on the notion that professional kindness and politeness by officers will allow drivers to perceive they are being treated in a fair manner. However, Epp et al. carefully demonstrate how this approach is insufficient, as black drivers can identify when they are being treated (un)fairly, independent of officer character. Specifically, the authors document narrative accounts showing that even when officers are kind, black drivers still feel unfairly treated when they are subjected to intrusive investigatory stops. Thus, they make the argument that citizen perceptions are influenced by the calculated decisions front-line bureaucratic actors make and the policies backing those decisions. Another tenet of procedural justice theory relates to how bureaucratic behavior influences citizen perceptions of their place in society. Rather than challenging this principle, the authors of Pulled Over use it to support a key component of their argument. Here, Epp et al. contend that investigatory stops communicate to black citizens a “second-class citizenship” that is of diminished quality in comparison to white citizens. A caveat to the conceptual framework is the subtle implicit theories relied upon but not explicitly mentioned, particularly as it relates to public management and organizational theory. For instance, throughout the book, the authors reference the role of courts in determining the legitimacy of police practices; discuss how support from researchers, professional associations, and other groups enabled the furtherance of investigatory stops; and cite the potential power litigation and media (among many things) have in changing the police bureaucracy to display how the external environment influences the police department. By doing this, the authors show the interplay between larger systems, institutional practices, and bureaucrat behavior, all of which clearly evidences an open systems approach to public administration (Thompson 1967). Furthermore, the authors dedicate a significant portion of the book to understanding how officers make decisions in regards to pulling citizens over, ticketing, or further investigating citizens. The authors highlight the wide range of administrative discretion officers have; absent from this discussion, however, are decision-making theories. Yet, the authors do mention that investigatory stops happen in a rational manner by the bureaucrat. Lipsky’s (1980) street-level bureaucracy theory, although dated, could have been added to the discussion of policy implementation and how practices become incognito policy. Lastly, the authors discuss the costs associated with the practice of investigatory stops including racial disparities in stops, minorities facing diminished perceptions of their citizenship and police legitimacy, and the creation of racial divides in communities. These costs could tie into larger discussions of performance management and how we measure outcomes and evaluate bureaucracies particularly as it relates to race, equity, and human, social costs. Yet, even without a discussion of the aforementioned theoretical frameworks, Pulled Over still manages to captivate the reader. In the concluding chapter, Epp et al. present a proposal for reform focused on racial justice. The authors challenge the reader to consider how wide racial disparities in other areas of the public service (apart from policing) can be attributed to institutionalized practices. Moreover, in detailing various changes that can be made to improve police-community relations, the authors highlight the importance of ending the practice of investigatory stops due to the resulting racial injustice and social costs. Altogether, their proposal touches on issues central to public management including organizational leadership, organizational culture and norms, rules governing practice, translating policy to practice, oversight procedures, training, and changes in external laws and criminal justice policy. The authors address their own limitations well, namely their focus on black and white citizens. However, they mention the applicability of their work to immigrants and Latinos. They also touch on issues of generalizability and how their findings are applicable outside of Kansas City. They note that similar studies conducted in other locales have found racial disparities in police stops and that investigatory stops are not unique to Kansas City but were implemented nationwide. Nonetheless, Pulled Over challenges some of the existing scholarship in public administration that pertains to race as well as the notion of an unbiased, neutral administrator. Pulled Over also challenges traditional approaches of measuring bureaucrat behavior by including both racial equity and public perceptions as outcome measures. Rather than merely acknowledging that racial disparities are present, this book encourages us to consider why these disparities exist and how they can be addressed. The text compliments work like Gooden’s (2014) book on race, equity, and government that advances a similar argument (e.g., that racism is systemic and deeply rooted in public administration). Gooden illustrates how variance in bureaucrat behavior is tolerated by upper level management, particularly when discretion exists, which then affects service distribution. Gooden also demonstrates the importance of looking at racial equity as an outcome in and of itself. Additionally, Epp et al. take the field of public administration back to its interdisciplinary roots by challenging scholars to consider other disciplinary perspectives when explaining bureaucrat behavior and agency outcomes. Furthermore, Pulled Over bridges practitioners and scholars because it is written on a topic that is salient across the country while providing work that is methodologically sound. Overall, the narrative approach coupled with the data visualization allows the material to be easily digested and understood. As a final point, it is important to note that policing has received much more scholarly attention in other academic fields in comparison to public administration.
