However, Maynard-Moody and Musheno (2003) show that police are government agents who operate within highly bureaucratic confines and perform duties based on policy operatives but who also have a high level of discretionary power. Therefore, the attention given to police in Pulled Over by public administration and political science scholars is well-fitting. Moreover, while Pulled Over is focused on policing specifically, a discussion of these findings in the context of the larger bureaucracy and the implications thereof is still necessary. Future research should also explore how this work can be applied to other substantive areas within the public sector.

t: Gary Miller and Andrew Whitford’s “Above Politics: Bureaucratic Discretion and Credible Commitment”
abs: In Gary Miller and Andrew Whitford’s Above Politics: Bureaucratic Discretion and Credible Commitment, the authors brilliantly reconsider the cluster of theories most frequently used to examine “bureaucratic control” (collectively known as Principal-Agent Theory [PAT]). To say that this is all they do, however, sells this impressive contribution short. Miller and Whitford force us to think carefully in both logical and empirically grounded terms about the “confrontation” between professional bureaucrats and elected officials in a separation of powers system and its implications for the viability of our democratic institutions. In doing so, they offer not only a rousing defense of professionalism but also a sobering lesson in our current political environment. Since Woodrow Wilson’s introduction of the field of public administration to American political science, a debate continues over the extent to which the US bureaucracy is (or should be) a subordinate institution subject to popular control by way of elected officials’ preferences. Concomitantly, the US administrative state has developed into a complex array of institutions that internally embody the fragmentation of its separation of powers political system. Each organization has been authorized autonomy to some relative degree through legislative, executive, or judicial authorization. In doing so, each implements, enforces, and creates policy. The base normative question, of course, is how do we balance the inherent autonomy and political power bureaus accumulate as a function of (and necessity to) their expertise (c.f., Gailmard and Patty 2012) while maintaining their accountability to the public will? The debate over this confrontation was most eloquently posed in 1940 between Carl Friedrich and Herman Finer. Over the last four decades, adherents to the Finerian concern of bureaucratic moral hazard have colonized the positivist tradition of political science and public management (Spence 2009). This hierarchical, top-down perspective primarily derived from the microeconomic perspective of PAT, which political scientists adopted in the late 1970s. Constructing bureaucratic politics as a complex of contractual relationships, the major focus of this scholarship has been to determine and anticipate the bureaucratic behavior and responsiveness to the preferences of political principals (i.e., almost exclusively executives and legislatures). Researchers in this tradition ask how much control these principals have over the bureaucracy, the extent to which bureaucratic moral hazard can be prevented, and the informational symmetry or advantages political principals can achieve vis-à-vis the bureaucratic agent. Every theory’s assumptions lead to abstraction. Arguably, the application of PAT to bureaucratic delegation has had rather limited empirical success. As Miller and Whitford set out to examine PAT’s contribution to the study of regulation, bureaucratic delegation, and institutions generally, they expose what they conceive as a fatal flaw in PAT approaches to the study of public bureaucracies. Their argument, in the end, strongly endorses Friedrich’s more nuanced prescription—one far less obsessed with accountability mechanisms imposed by political actors and more focused on emphasizing “professional discretion, credible commitment, and trust” (p. 16). Miller and Whitford responds with a theoretical adaptation that aptly balances the line between the realistic and the elegant. The implicit normative concern in common applications of PAT to bureaucratic delegation leads to a distinct focus on the agent’s moral hazard [in which an expert bureaucracy imposes North’s (1981) social costs of dictatorship]. Instead, Miller and Whitford conceptualize the relationship as a tradeoff in which we might fear the political moral hazard inherent in principals’ short-term incentives that can undermine the stability of markets and clear property rights necessary for economic growth (i.e., North’s social costs of disorder). Miller and Whitford flip the traditional PAT paradigm on its head, as they posit “the more fundamental role for bureaucracy is not to be tamed by politicians, but to constrain them. Bureaucracies can play their most important role as part of a system of checks and balances” (p. 21). Miller and Whitford in many ways introduce a concept that is common in normative public administration theory but largely ignored in the “bureaucratic control” scholarship: the professional administrator as a trustee. While their model certainly allows for the possibility that bureaucrats can and do violate this role, the introduction of political moral hazard to the traditional PAT model provides a complication that severely hamstrings the plausibility of its traditional assumptions as applied to bureaucratic politics. Because political moral hazard exists, the introduction of that hazard has a balancing effect on the likelihood of its counterpart—bureaucratic moral hazard. Simply put, both bureaucrats and politicians constrain their own proclivities toward moral hazard in order to achieve a tradeoff. As Miller and Whitford see it, however, politicians are far more susceptible to violating this pact. Therefore (evoking Herbert Kauffman and Dan Carpenter), the key to upholding credible commitment is the professional identity and reputation of the bureaus. Not only does professionalism infuse internal checks on bureaus that give politicians an ability to reasonably predict behavior, but it provides the bureaus with a powerful political stratagem that, in turn, checks the politicians—they are perceived as (and convey themselves as) “Above Politics.” The book is organized to methodically structure the authors’ argument in a way that makes it accessible to those either steeped in or unfamiliar with established scholarship in bureaucratic delegation. Importantly, Miller and Whitford incorporate and leverage a bevy of insights from institutional economics, political economy, and economic history that crisply reveal their points. The first chapter provides an entertaining encapsulation of their theory through the example of the Keating Five in the 1980s Savings and Loan crisis. This serves to unload the key observations made throughout the book that (1) society critically depends on the professionalism of bureaucratic agents to check political moral hazard because (2) political principals are often not credible in their commitment to good governance or the public interest; further, (3) both bureaucrats and politicians are checked by the extent to which bureaus are instilled with professional norms. The second chapter provides a review of PAT and the many contributions to understanding delegation dilemmas that it has provided. As much as Miller and Whitford reveal fundamental flaws in the framework, its application has yielded important insights to the structural effectiveness of the US federal system, the democratic legitimacy of the bureaucracy, and the symbiotic relationships of political institutions in a separation of powers system. Indeed, in many respects Miller and Whitford incorporate the tools that PAT offers to their attempt at a more cohesive and contextually flexible theory. Nonetheless, as they shift to Chapters 3 and 4, Miller and Whitford convincingly deconstruct an empirical reality that is ignored in the assumptions of many PAT adherents: the time inconsistent preferences of politicians. With this in mind, the authors employ Holmström’s (1982) impossibility theorem that there is no jointly produced good that can achieve both Nash equilibrium and Pareto efficiency because incentives will inevitably vary among team members. Therefore, we find a continuum of variation in how agencies are shaped: some are shaped to carry out principals’ objectives that are ripe with susceptibility to political moral hazard whereas others are insulated in order to limit political moral hazard and maximize bureaucratic autonomy. Chapter 5 explains why we see this variation. After all, as the authors note, “we cannot assume that politicians turn suddenly altruistic—giving up authority to bureaucrats because of a desire to do the right thing” (p. 99). The key to this puzzle (why politicians grant bureaucrats autonomy at all) follows Moe’s (1989) thesis that bureaucracies are not created out of the interest of carrying out the public will, but out of political compromise that prevents one’s enemy from control. This chapter expounds Whitford’s previous work on bureaucracies in a separation of powers system, in which the multiple principals dilemma must be accommodated in PAT more explicitly. For those familiar with Miller and Whitford’s past collaborations and respective individual work, one distinguishing feature of this book is the melding and maturation of these works into one smartly developed and unified thesis. For instance, Whitford’s multiple principals treatment, by itself, is limited in explaining why a principal so often fails at realizing his objectives when an agency is indeed shaped with the intention to carry out that principal’s political preferences. Accordingly, the subsequent two chapters continue Miller’s influential work on the “control paradox” in PAT. Essentially, in order to prevent bureaucratic moral hazard, political principals institute strict hierarchy, monitoring mechanisms, and exceptionally detailed rules. Yet, the lack of trust that these efforts signal to the agent induces reciprocal distrust and limited incentives for the agent to follow through on the political principal’s goals (Resh 2015). At the same time, when a principal relaxes its control, this allows for deference to the agent’s professional identity which, in turn, helps define the identity of the organization and expands autonomy. To put it differently, some bureaucratic autonomy and deference to professionalism must be allowed in this relationship in order to see through the principal’s preferences to some extent. Professionalism, in turn, provides an internal check to the bureau to constrain their own behavior; hence, it both delimits and motivates behavior by both the principal and the agent to provide stability and limit social costs in either direction. That is to say, bureaucracies provide essential Madisonian checks on the ambitions of politicians through the mechanism of professional expertise. The authors continue by leveraging historical evidence of the constant tension in the tradeoff between politicians and professionals by examining the record of financial regulation in the United States from the days of Glass-Steagall to the 2008 crisis and the undoing of key sections in the Dodd-Frank Act. Here, we find time and again the most likely violators of credible commitment to a stable and fair market are not the bureaucracies charged with regulating market actors, but politicians who seek to intervene for the good of specific market actors in response to prevailing—but shortsighted—electoral pressures. As I write this review, an anti-professional, populist sentiment helps propel a new US presidential administration into office. With this transition as context, one can draw rather bleak predictions from Miller and Whitford’s book. Early presidential nominees for cabinet positions have indicated disproportionate favoritism to particular market segments, with the president-elect publicly intervening on behalf of specific market actors and explicitly vilifying others. Some nominees and the president-elect himself have professed an outright rejection of various positions supported by a preponderance of scientific or professional expertise. A tangible resentment of the professional class by many in the electoral coalition that carried the administration into office substantially emboldens its stance. While Whitford’s original observation that a stalemate among political institutions enables the additional check of administrative professionalism to our Madisonian system, the authors also warn that a separation of powers must hold to ensure credible commitment between politicians and bureaus. When these powers are aligned electorally by party and ideology, bureaucratic autonomy can be considerably compromised. Moreover, in a highly partisan political environment in which each side seeks to confirm its priors and has a plethora of sources available for exactly that purpose, is it reasonable to assume that bureaucrats can “act with assurance that any professional of good standing would see the facts largely as they did” and it would matter as it did in the Keating Five case (p. 8)? It is to this contemporary point that I would have liked a deeper exploration into the emergence of anti-intellectualism in the United States over the last half-century and its apparent explosion in the age of the internet and the exponential growth in partisan outlets. This culminating backlash against institutions and, especially, the professional class did not emerge in just one election cycle or as a convenience to political opportunism. The authors argue that the volatility of preferences shaped through legislative and electoral politics gravely threatens the stability of markets and the transparency of property rights. Yet, there is a tangible, persistent, and purposeful strain of anti-intellectualism that pervades American politics. Is it, instead, the administrative state’s “emphasis on legal-technical rationality, bureaucratization, and professionalization [that has marginalized] citizens from their government, evoking images of Weber’s dilettantes facing an expert bureaucracy” (Durant and Ali 2013, 278)? Has the professional class in public administration failed in reconciling the complexities of policy with its ethical responsibility of informing and empowering the citizen? The authors, at least implicitly, assume universal deference to professional opinions, if administrators are not constrained unnecessarily by politicians. I believe the authors are brutally correct in their assessment of political moral hazard as a far graver threat to undermining the credible commitment of our institutional system. Therefore, I do not fault the authors for emphasizing its menace because it serves as an accurate and long-needed correction to the foundational assumptions in PAT and the bureaucratic control scholarship. This, in itself, makes it a seminal contribution. Nonetheless, a professionalized administrative state is not, by itself, a panacea. It is, as the authors reveal, a convincing and critical ballast in the US separation of powers system. On the other hand, if we accept the inevitability of political moral hazard, then it seems that missing from either account is the ethical responsibility of administrators beyond their respective professional roles to engage directly the public outside the channel of elected officials—i.e., an active rather than passive strategy of “above politics” is more frequently required. For, if professionalized bureaucrats are resource-starved, their opinions muffled, their organizational lives politicized, and their standing consistently bashed for purely political gains, then we, indeed, face Miller and Whitford’s (and by proxy Madison’s) central fear that political moral hazard is not sufficiently checked.

t: The Orchestration of Potentiality: Finding the Remedy for Public Management Dilemmas
abs: The aim of this book is ambitious—to offer a theory of managing public organizations in an era of paradoxes, where the need for governance remains as strong as ever, yet the tasks of governing must coexist with a constant need for adaptability, transformation, and innovativeness. Crucially, this theory seeks to adopt a broader definition of “public management” by venturing outside the typical portrayal of bureaucracies as something inherently and consistently objective, competent, and independent of their contexts. Governance is viewed in a broader lens, where research of the state and society are fundamentally intertwined with public management research (and outcomes) broadly defined. Indeed, a series of recent essays in Governance ask the same question—“Is Public Management Neglecting the State?” Eight short commentaries tackle various aspects of such neglect—“Does it neglect important questions about the development of major institutions of the modern state? Has it focused unduly on problems of advanced democracies? Has it made itself irrelevant to public debates about the role and design of government, and the capacity of public institutions to deal with emerging challenges?” (Milward et al. 2016). The need for answering these questions is obvious, and the book by Andersen and Pors is on the cutting edge of this effort. The book is well-balanced with concerns for generalizability—to synthesize a concept that can be applied to a broader field of public management (applied to any specific single or cross-functional area that experiences inputs from and influences all participants in a welfare state) or any level of analysis simultaneously (applied at societal, state, organizational, and individual levels). In their own words, the goal is to understand “the ‘machine’ that drives the whole management field in the public sector, and that continues to compel us to seek out new ways of management. We are not simply looking for solutions to problems; we are also looking for the machine that produces the problems and that connects them to the solutions. We ask: what is the problem that particular problem-solution combinations in welfare management function as a solution for” (p. 1). The “machine” fosters potentiality—an ability to address both current and potential dilemmas by commanding many solutions. “Potentialization is about creating possibilities for change beyond the presently imaginable” (p. 22). The ultimate “machine” in the public sector is expected to generate potentiality in four areas. First, public sector managers are expected to ensure case quality but must remain open to the notion that the varying definitions of the case and perspectives of participants may yield numerous potential solutions. Thus, the authors argue that factuality is contingent, not fixed. Second, as public sector managers operate in multidisciplinary settings, they must expect that different professional approaches may yield differing potential solutions. This underscores the position that professional knowledge is contingent, not fixed. Third, public sector managers are expected to nurture employees who continually develop skills and perspectives to take complete charge over their membership role in the organization and to continually provide potential solutions. This, the authors argue, results in self-membership under contingent conditions, not fixed membership. Fourth, public managers cannot rely on fixed solutions or approaches, as there are numerous potential perspectives that exist, which may yield multiple possible choices. Therefore, the argument is that there exist multiple contingent wholes, not a fixed whole. Andersen and Pors excel in applying the concept of potentiality to differing contingencies and levels of analysis. A natural question nonetheless remains: Is potentiality a remedy for public management dilemmas broadly defined? To what extent can and should potentiality be applied to all problems, both simple and complex? In this regard, the book can be placed among the latest works on the theories of governance, or “new” models of governance as discussed in Frederickson et al. (2012), where “the governance debate simply shows that academics are catching up to the reality of changed times. The rise of the fragmented state and the growing obsolescence of existing public management frameworks have forced the discipline to undertake a sometimes painful search for new intellectual foundations” (p. 234). The book by Andersen and Pors can perhaps be nicely complemented by Lynn, Heinrich, and Hill’s (2001) book on empirical research in governance. In their reduced form of governance, the latter authors wrote that the outcomes of governance could be parameterized by factors such as environmental features, client characteristics, treatments, structures, and managerial roles and actions. Such reduced form is necessary for conducting empirical studies by finding a handle on parts of complexity. While Andersen and Pors do an excellent job of discussing how problems and solutions ought to be evaluated at multiple levels of analysis, which in turn offers numerous potential research questions to interested scholars, their book is less about designing research on how to operationalize potentiality or about how to measure the antecedents and consequences of potentiality. Many concepts of public sector governance outcomes and the factors associated with them are offered, yet the readers must develop their own approaches to measuring and analyzing them. Thus, the book is a superb source for generating research questions, but not necessarily for how to go about evaluating and analyzing them. Even so, how does one study the “machine” of problems and solutions when factuality is contingent, knowledge is contingent, and membership is contingent—all possibly subject to multiple wholes? Admittedly, this book does not identify the development of measures and constructs as one of their goals. This only makes a book by Lynn, Heinrich, and Hill (2001)—or any other book similar to it—an indispensable complement to Andersen and Pors. Undoubtedly, the work by Andersen and Pors is an exciting and refreshing way of looking at public management practices. Yet, missed opportunities, elements that should have been a part of the discussion, must be emphasized as well. The language on orchestration of potentiality implies that there is a conductor that is in charge of the orchestra. While individual musicians are extremely talented and versatile, they play music in their sections (i.e., strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion). The conductor’s role is to ensure that each individual musician’s talents are utilized to the greatest extent and that the different sections of the orchestra combine to produce beautiful music rather than disjointed cacophony of sounds. The conductor’s role is, therefore, to lead—to release individual, section, and orchestra potentiality. There are decades of leadership research, both from the private and public sectors, which would have been of greatest resource if incorporated in the book. Van Wart’s (2003) call for an integrated approach to leadership or Lawler’s (2008) recommendations to move toward distributed or collective leadership in the private sector would have been a good place start. Furthermore, Andersen and Pors describe how orchestration of potentiality has surfaced as the only viable option compared to previous approaches to governance—rule-, planning-, and supervision-based approaches to public sector management. Specifically, the main advantage is that “Potentiality administration seeks to facilitate a form of independence where institutions continually confront themselves by reflecting on whether a given action, service or procedure might be carried out differently, might be rethought. It introduces new contingency into public administration. The mindset is everywhere and always: it could be different” (p. 85). Prior research, for example by Simon (1989) or Aiken and Hage (1971), has shown evidence of the limits of individuals and organizations—whether informational or technological. Assuming potentialization is a higher-order solution, what are the limits on capacities of public sector organizations? Or are there possible incomplete outcomes due to bounded potentialization or bounded orchestration of potentiality? Or is full potentiality absolutely necessary at all times? An inclusion of prior work on the limits surrounding public sector organizations would have enriched the discussion on the need and role for potentiality administration. To be sure, the core elements that are necessary for management applications are skillfully articulated in the book. Scholars and practitioners of public sector management should not feel discouraged to fill in the gaps using existing research and practices as necessary (and remember that their facts and knowledge may be contingent, not fixed). At the same time, I share Walker’s (2011) optimism that the field of public management, both as a localized and global discipline, is developing in the right direction. “We have much excitement to look forward to over coming years—the agenda for future scholarship is open and wide and is ripe for the taking as interdisciplinary design science questions based on either policy or practice or stemming from intellectual curiosity abound” (p. 58). The book by Andersen and Pors is certainly an outstanding testimony of such progress.

t: Direct Democracy and Administrative Disruption
abs: Direct democracy is often touted as a means of reining in the administrative state, but it could also hinder the performance of public organizations. In particular, we argue that bargaining dynamics between voters and government officials can lead to costly administrative disruptions. We explore this issue by estimating the impact of Ohio tax referenda on school district administration using a regression discontinuity approach. The results suggest that administrators in districts where referenda failed sought to insulate core functions from revenue declines. Nonetheless, referendum failure (as opposed to passage) led to lower instructional spending, teacher attrition, and lower student achievement growth. Spending and performance generally rebounded within a few years, however, as districts eventually secured approval for a subsequent tax proposal. These results illustrate how involving citizens in decision-making can entail short-term transaction costs in the form of decreased administrative performance, which in this case may have had lasting achievement effects for students attending school in the wake of a referendum failure. Direkte Demokratie wird oft als ein Mittel beworben, um den Verwaltungsstaat in seine Schranken zu weisen. Allerdings könnte dabei auch die Leistungsfähigkeit der öffentlichen Verwaltung nachlassen. Wir argumentieren, dass die Verhandlungsdynamiken zwischen Wählern und Verwaltungsbeamten zu kostspieligen Beeinträchtigungen der Leistung der Verwaltung führen können. Dazu untersuchen wir mittels eines Regressions-Diskontinuitäts-Designs den Effekt von Steuerreferenda in Ohio auf die Schulbezirksverwaltung. Die Ergebnisse deuten darauf hin, dass Bezirke, in denen ein Referendum scheiterte, ihre Kernaufgaben gegen Einnahmeeinbußen abgeschirmt haben. Gleichwohl führten gescheiterte Referenda zu weniger Bildungsausgaben, Abwanderung von Lehrern und geringeren Steigerungen bei den Leistungen der Schüler. Die Ausgaben und Leistungen erholten sich jedoch nach ein paar Jahren, als die Schulbezirke die Zustimmung zu einem neuen Steuer-Vorschlag bekamen. Diese Ergebnisse zeigen, dass die Beteiligung von Bürgern kurzfristige Transaktionskosten in Form von verringerter Verwaltungsleistung erzeugen kann, die in diesem Fall einen nachhaltigen Effekt auf die Leistung der Schüler gehabt haben könnte, die nach einem gescheiterten Referendum die Schule besuchen.
